speechtext: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 73 to authorize the ratification and carrying into effect of the protocol of the sixteenth day of December, 1920, accepting the statute for the Permanent Court of International Justice of the thirteenth day of December, 1920.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister might explain this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Bill contains two clauses. The first provides for the ratification of the protocol referred to, and the other confers power to do such things as may be necessary to carry it out. The Assembly at Geneva unanimously assented to the proposed plan for the creation of a Permanent Court of International Justice, under the provisions of the Treaty and the Covenant of the League, in virtue whereof a plan had been prepared; and it was provided that the Council of the League should submit such a plan for adoption by the pations who are members of the League. While there was some difference of opinion upon the question, the view was entertained by a large portion of the representatives- I may say, the Canadian representatives shared in that view-that it was not competent for the representatives in the Assembly to assent on behalf of their respective countries to the adoption of the plan submitted. They were all satisfied with it, but took the view that the provisions of the Covenant required submission of the plan to the members of the League themselves, that is to say, the various nations, and adoption by them. Pursuant to this view, a protocol was drawn up for signature by the different nations through their representatives, which protocol was made subject to ratification by the nations signing. Canada has signed the protocol subject to ratification. While, of course, the power of ratification is in the Crown, acting on the advice of its constitutional advisers, at the same time it is considered proper and desirable that the executive should not take upon itself to ratify without the authorization of

Parliament, and this Bill is submitted containing the provisions I have stated,-first, to authorize the ratification of the protocol, and second, to authorize the doing of the necessary things to carry it out. There will be found, annexed to the Bill as a schedule, the resolution of the Assembly, the protocol itself, which has been signed, and the statute, as it is called, containing the plan constituting the Court. That plan was, in the first place, prepared under the direction of the Council, and was accepted by the Council with certain amendments unanimously agreed to by the Assembly.

What extra
expense will this involve?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: None.
May I ask what would happen should the Canadian Parliament fail to ratify this protocol?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If we should fail to
ratify the protocol Canada would not have approved the constitution of the Court, and would therefore not be entitled to invoke its jurisdiction or appear before it.
It would not necessarily mean the resignation of the Government, I hope?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would not consider that that would be implied. However, I am not apprehensive of that condition arising. I count upon the good judgment of my hon. friend, among others, to assure us that so desirable a project will be ratified.
I was not here when the right hon. gentleman began his explanation, and I rise for the purpose of asking whether the United States has agreed to be represented on that Court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The United States was not represented at the Assembly and is therefore not called upon to take part in this ratification. It is, however, provided under the terms of the plan, or constitution establishing the Court, that countries mentioned in the schedule to the Covenant shall have access to that Court. The Court will therefore be open to the United States event though that country should not become a member of the League. I am not in a position to express any view as to what the action of the United States is likely to be. It is perhaps noteworthy that a very prominent part of the preparation of the constitution of the Court was

taken by one of the most distinguished lawyers of the United States, and that, so far as one can judge from the press, even those who did not warmly favour the League of Nations have expressed themselves in the highest terms with regard to the establishment of this Court.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) :
speechtext: Discussion of the measure may properly be deferred until the Bill has been printed. There is, however, one thing I desire to ask my right hon. friend. In answer to a question from this side the minister said there will be no expense involved. This is purely an honorary court is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I was asked what
expense would be involved for Canada.
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Provision is made for payment of the expenses in connection with the Court of the League of Nations, but our contribution to the expenses of the League is determined under a clause of the covenant itself.
On the Postal Union basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, on the Postal Union basis. In that connection I may say that it would appear to be quite settled that there will be a modification of the rule as regards the expenses generally which will undoubtedly result in a reduction of the contribution imposed upon Canada. I think I am safe in saying that, because there was a general recognition that the application * of the distribution of costs as established by the Postal Union operated inequitably as regards the League of Nations. It was quite understood that there should be a revision, and that that revision when it was made should so retroact as to make good any sums in excess that may have been paid under the existing provision.

If I may submit
another question: I understood my hon. friend to say that Canada will pay, but through the League of Nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, but will not pay anything more than its contribution to the League of Nations.
That contribution has been fixed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It has been fixed but will be revised in the manner I have described.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: Mr. H. M. MOW AT (Parkdale) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 74 to amend the Criminal Code (Probation of Offenders).
Explain.

The code contains the provision for "suspended sentence." This Bill extends the provision to "probation." The probation system is now concurred in by all experienced judges and magistrates. The confirmed criminal usually commences with some petty offence. If you brand him then as a convict, you will probably assist him to a downward career. If you commit him to the friendly, but authoritative, care of a probation officer appointed by a province or a municipality you may save him for society. The percentages of reclamation under the "probation" system have been large.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

I am being asked a good many questions about the income tax; there seems to be considerable dissatisfaction with the manner in which it is being collected. Under the present system a man is obliged to assess himself, and then when he fills out his form he must send with it a certain percentage of his tax-twenty-five per cent I think-and the balance must be sent at the rate of so much a month for the next couple of months. The thing that seems wrong about that is this: a person makes out the form, as he thinks, correctly, he finds that his tax is $60 and he sends one quarter of that, $15, with his filled-out form and it goes into the tax collector's office. They go over the form and find that the tax should be $64; therefore they find that he has failed to send in the twenty-five per cent as required by law. He is short one dollar and they have no recourse except to subject him to a fine. I find quite a number of persons objecting to this form of collection. They think-and I must say that I agree with them-that the tax office should make the assessment, and should send a man his bill showing how much tax he should pay, and if he thinks they are wrong he should in all fairness have an opportunity to take the matter up and discuss it with them. But to oblige him to assess himself and then subject him to a fine if he makes a mistake strikes me as manifestly unfair, illogical, and wrong all through. I do not think it should be done in this way at all. I do not know who is responsible for the idea. Many people who have to make out these forms have had no legal training and are not chartered accountants, and because of their liability to fine they go to others who are supposed to have expert knowledge and get them to make out their forms or assist them in making them out. This, of course, involves the payment of a fee. I am credibly informed that a member of the staff of the tax collector's office at Hamilton-I do not know how long he had been on the staff- gave up his position there and opened an office as expert adviser to those who were finding difficulty in making out their tax forms. Well, if a man can leave a fairly good job and find it advantageous to open up an office to assist men who are meeting with difficulty in making out their income tax returns, it does seem to me that a strong effort should be made to simplify the forms. Is it the intention of the Government to continue this present system of

collecting the income tax, or is a change contemplated?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The department is trying to make the collection of income tax a reality; to have everybody pay who ought to pay. I frankly confess that any task of that kind is both unpopular and difficult. The department is also endeavouring to keep down the cost of collection and to take in a maximum amount of money with a minimum of outlay, also to render the bills, because finally they have to be rendered so that liabilities may be met, at the same time for everybody in the country. In order to do that, and in the first instance, to keep down expense, if we are going to save the very-large amount of interest that in the past has been lost, we must get the bills out at a very much earlier date. Hon. gentlemen know that while in the past returns have been made out in the spring, bills have not been sent out until the late autumn, and that, even then, bills have not been sent out to everybody at the same time; there have been delays. The real reason, of course, is simply this, that on the returns being made, those returns have to be checked, and after that bills have to be sent out. If we had a sufficient staff to do all that work quickly and to get out all those bills together, the cost of collecting the tax would be very serious, I am afraid. We are trying then to get returns in at an early date and, in order to save interest, to get in as much money as possible, and yet not increase unduly the cost of collection. To do this involves the ratepayer doing, in the first instance, what he has always done, that is make out the return which shows his real income, and after having made out that return, pay twenty-five per cent of what he ought to pay under it. My hon. friend is quite right. There are serious penalities in the Act; but those penalities do not apply to mistakes or errors of judgment, they are directed to false returns. In other words, the penalities apply to that part of the matter which the ratepayer ought to know about, namely, what is his income, not to any error that he may make in forwarding his initial contribution. This method of taxation is not a new one; a similar method applies in the United States, and it is a method which, if it had been applied earlier in Canada, ought to have materially assisted the country's finance without unduly hurting or, indeed, at all hurting the ratepayer.

Do they make collections in the United States in the same manner?
TMr. Edwards.]

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. I admit there is a great deal of doubt and uncertainty about the thing, but there always is in connection with anything that is new. In order to get rid of that doubt and uncertainly, I have got out those special instructions which have been widely distributed, and I do not think anybody need be at much difficulty in making out the tax returns with those special instructions before them. But if they are wrong simply in the computation, as I said before, they are not in any way subject to the severe penalities prescribed by the Act.

The Act says that they are subject. Why are they not? Is the minister going to continue the collection of the taxes as mapped out in the Act of last year? We have to forward our returns by April 30, and if we are wrong, we are subject to a fine; the Act says that we are.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have been
unfortunate in not making myself clear. The return has to be put in, and if the return is a false one, if information is kept back, if the income is greater than represented, the heavy penalties prescribed by the Act attach. But those penalties, as I have said before, do not attach to errors made in the computation of the taxes due on that income. As I said before, in answer to questions already put, it is the intention of the Government to bring down, at this session of Parliament, an Act which is now on the Order Paper and which would have been proceeded with before now, had it not been for the pressure of other business and the impossibility of getting on with it. It has been pointed out that we have more employees. We have, and perhaps I ought to give to the House a little information in connection with what we are doing as regards income tax.
I will not go back very far. Of course, the great thing is to get your collections in as quickly and as regularly as you can in order to save interest, and to try to get the money quickly and equitably from everybody in the country. In 1919-20 the total collection of income tax up to February 28, 1920, was $9,982,140. The total collected this year up to February 28, amounted to $32,666,940. Let us take the next ten-day group. Last year, up to March 10, 1920, the total collected was over $11,-000,000-I do not give the odd figures: the total collected up to the same date of this year was $35,000,000. On March 20, the next ten-day period, the total collected last year was $11,000,000 and this year it was $36,000,000. The figures are not quite complete up to the end of the fiscal year,

because there are always payments which come in from the outside and which take a little time after March 31, before they are taken into the books; but if we deal merely with payments which were taken into the books on March 31, last year, the total amount collected was $17,000,000, and this year it was $38,000,000. It costs us, of course, a little more to collect $38,000,000 than it did to collect $17,000,000, and we hope to improve further the collection.

I wish to ask a question; but before doing so, I should like to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) if he takes the ground that all departments are open for discussion without a motion to go into Supply on departments that have not already been considered. Because I do not wish to put a question on a department that has not been considered properly before, unless it is the intention of the Government to take the ground that we are or will be in Supply on any item that the Government chooses to take up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The question is a
question for the Chair at the proper time. It is not a question for the Prime Minister. We are not in Supply now, but in Committee of the Whole on the Bill, and the question does not affect what we are doing at all.

I wish to ask the Prime
Minister what he meant last night when he said:
We are ready for all Supply now, except that we will not go into External Affairs.
He must have meant something; I do not suppose he is always joking; and I want to know what he meant by that statement last night.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I meant exactly what
I said. It is the intention of the Government to go into any Supply except External Affairs. The Estimates of some departments have passed. We are ready with the others. If objection is taken, we can decide the matter then. That question has nothing to do with the Bill upon which we are now in Committee of the Whole.

I think it has. If the
Government take the ground, and they are sustained by the Chair, that all departments have been moved into Supply and that they can therefore take up the Estimates of any department on a Thursday or Friday without a motion that the Speaker do leave the Chair, that might have a considerable bearing on this Bill. I would like to know the attitude of the Government on that question. It is not so much
the ruling of the Chair as the attitude of the Government that I want to know. I would like 'an answer.

The ruling that the
Chairman should give at the present time is that the question asked by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) is not relevant to the clause which is now under consideration. The Committee is discussing clause 2 of the interim Supply Bill and the debate must be relevant to the clause. In fact there are greater limitations to the rights of hon. members upon the different stages of an Appropriation Bill than is the case upon other bills. Subjects involving expenditure which is not provided for by the Bill cannot be suggested and discussed. The conduct of the officials or of the departments who receive the supply grants cannot be challenged. Amendments cannot be moved to clauses or schedules to effect the omission of an item or the reduction of the amount of any grant or an alteration in the destination of any grant. The enacting words of the bill cannot be amended. Subject to the above limitations, hon. members have the right to ask questions concerning all matters for which grants are provided by the bill now before the Committee. The Chairman cannot at this time give any other ruling.

I quite agree with your
ruling, Mr. Chairman. I do not want to delay the committee by asking questions now, if it is understood that the different departments will be moved into Supply as has been the practice in the past. Otherwise, we will have no opportunity of knowing what is to be taken up from day to day, and as the Prime Minister knows now that the committees are sitting while the House is in session, it is impossible for hon. members to attend to their duties in the committees and at the same time be present in the House when Estimates in which they are interested are taken up. I wish to know what the Prime Minister intends to do in the future. It is quite possible that he has the right under his closure methods to take up any department at any time, and jump from one department to another just as he pleases. I do not wish to ask the Prime Minister to reply to anything that is not within the rules, but if we knew what the procedure would be, I think it might facilitate the passage of this Bill. There are a number of questions I would like to put now if I am to be precluded from putting them later. If the Prime Minister would say that it is not

his intention to break away from the usual practice, I do not think we would find it necessary to put quite so many questions at the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think I understand
what the hon. member wants. He wants to know if notice is to be given of the Supply we intend to go into each day, so that he will be able to be present.

If my right hon.
friend will permit me, what my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), and what I myself also, want to know is whether all the departments will be considered as having been taken up once this Bill is passed; whether the Government will be at liberty to take up the Estimates of any department on Thursdays and Fridays even if they have not been taken pp previously.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If the hon. member
wants my opinion, I have no objection to giving it. I gave it the other day. My opinion is that as hon. gentlemen insisted that the interim Supply had that effect on Thursdays and Fridays, the rule must necessarily work both ways, and the Government has that right. I pointed that out at the time. I have no objection to giving my opinion. I say frankly now to the hon. gentleman that that would necessarily be the effect, in my view. I am not asking the Chair to rule on it, because the question really does not come up now.

My right hon. friend knows that in previous years interim Supply was always granted after an understanding between the parties, and that it never interfered with the rights of the Opposition with regard to motions of want of confidence on days when the House had to be moved into Committee of Supply.
I think it always took place on some other day than Thursday or Friday, so that question did not arise.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have answered that. I say that in my view we undoubtedly have that right.

I am glad to see my hon. friend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne) in his seat. Not long ago there was a judgment of the Privy Council altering the respective positions of the Federal Government and the provinces as regards the fisheries. I understand that under this judgment the department of my hon. friend, from May 1, next, will issue the licenses for salmon fishing in the lower St. Lawrence-I am speaking for my own constituency and that of my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil). I wanted to know whether my hon. friend intends to appoint fishery officers for that purpose, and not only in connection with the salmon fisheries but other fisheries which hitherto	have been under
the jurisdiction	of the provinces.
I want to know, first, whether my hon. friend will appoint, or has appointed, new fishery officers; and, secondly, whether he will not consider the desirability of renewing, in favour of the same persons, the salmon licenses that have been held by certain families from time immemorial. In my opinon it would be a grave injustice if, because the control of these licenses has been transferred from the Provincial Government to the federal authorities, the old holders of salmon licenses were deprived of rights which they have enjoyed for such a long time. I hope my hon. friend will not regard as extinct the rights in this matter of the people of the counties of Bonaventure and Gaspe. The salmon stands in my province are situated chiefly in these two counties, and I hope the minister will renew the licenses in favour of the old holders.

I may be
dense, but I should be glad if the hon. member would explain what connection there is between salmon fishing and the subject before the committee.

We are voting one-sixth of the Supply, which includes fisheries, the payment of salaries, disbursements to fish-

ery officers, etc.; and I notice an increase of $44,000 on a particular item, evidently to cover the additional expenditure entailed by the judgment of the Privy Council. My hon. friend should look at item 237 in the Estimates. I do not rise to delay the business of the House, but I think that information on the point I have raised, which is important, should be given, in the interests of my constituency, before this is carried.

I want my hon. friend to understand that I have not the slightest objection to the point he has raised so long as it is in accordance with the rules. I do not know, as a matter of fact, where we are; we cannot hear what is going on.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite right when he states that owing to a recent judgment of the Privy Council of England the fisheries of all tidal waters and navigable streams leading from the sea are now vested in the Federal Government. The Department of Marine and Fisheries on and after the first day of May, is going to take over the fisheries so allotted, and official notice has been sent through the proper channel to the Provincial Government. I am not yet prepared to say what we shall do with the old officials and fishery officers, nor do I know what the department will do in regard to the old licenses for salmon fishing or the catching of any other kind of fish to be found in these waters. Every consideration will be given to the old holders of these licenses, but I will not say that, because they have held these licenses for a long time, therefore, ipso facto, the department will renew them. All I can say is that due regard will be had to the length of time the licenses have been held.

I do not see why any change should be made in the present system as it applies to the Atlantic coast. The fisheries on that coast have been administered by the Federal Government for many years, and the fact that the Privy Council has now decided that the Federal Government has a right to administer the fisheries throughout the Dominion, should not disturb the conditions at present existing on the Atlantic coast. Do I understand that the decision of the Privy Council will make any difference in the administration of the law in the Maritime Provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That decision appertains to the province of Quebec. There has been for many years an outstanding difference between the province of Quebec and the Federal Government, and the change which my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) has brought to my attention does not in any way affect the rights of Nova Scotia.	*

The river Restigouehe separates Quebec from New Brunswick, and I understand that fishing rights on that river have been granted to many American capitalists as well as Canadians. That river being interprovincial, would the federal law not conflict with the provincial regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot add anything more to what I have already said. I think I have already made the situation clear as regards the province of Quebec. As regards New Brunswick, the fisheries in that province will be administered in the future as in the past, under the direction of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.	,

The minister does not understand me. The river Restigouehe is interprovincial, and under the present decision of the Privy Council the federal law will control the rights of fishing in this river, although for a considerable distance the river runs through Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The fisheries on this river, in the province of Quebec, will be administered in the same way as the federal authorities have administered the fisheries in Nova Scotia and New Bruns. wick.
That is to say, they will be administered as they were previous to the decision of the Privy Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the Prime Minister a question. Does he think that by moving this resolution for interim Supply, he circumvents the difficulty of moving on Tuesday or Wednesday to go into Supply? If he takes that position, what would prevent him from going into interim Supply, say, on April 1, if the House had met, let us say, on March 17? If the House had met on that day, and the Address had lasted until April 1, does he argue that he could then have moved a resolution for interim

Supply, before Supply had been moved at all? Does he think that by this ingenious method of closure he could obviate the necessity of moving that the Speaker leave the Chair for the House to go into Supply on Tuesday and Wednesday, and that he would then have the right to take up any items in any department he liked on Thursday and Friday, following that up with his closure if he wished to continue discussion from Thursday at three o'clock until he completed all Supply? Does the Prime Minister contend that it is within the rights of the Government, under the present rules, to do that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I understand precisely what my hon. friend desires to know, but I will put his question in a form that will make my answer better understood. It will be recalled that when the House took up, I think it was last Thursday, the question of interim Supply objection was raised by the Opposition on the ground that inasmuch as interim Supply spread the vote over all departments, and as some of the departments had not been taken up in Committee of Supply at all on Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday, we could not go on with interim Supply on Thursday.
I took the ground that it would be unwise to hold that that was the case, and that if it were the case technically, it would be unwise to follow such an interpretation, because it was out of harmony with the intent of the rules and if adopted would bring about this consequence:	that of
making it possible by going into interim Supply on Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday to virtually abrogate the whole rule because thereafter we could go in on any department on Thursday or Friday. Notwithstanding that I pointed out this consequence, and nothwithstanding the fact, which I still say is indisputable, that there was in reality, no more substantial objection to having interim Supply on Thursday than on Tuesday, hon. gentlemen opposite insisted on their course and' brought themselves into the position in which they are now. Therefore, I give my opinion-although when the issue comes up it is the Chairman who decides-that undoubtedly we have the right if we go into interim Supply on Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday, to go into Supply on any department at all covered by interim Supply on Thursday or Friday; undoubtedly that follows.
I give that as my opinion merely as to what the rule implies. Now let me add again: I do not think it was" ever the Plr. Cahill.]
intention of the rules that that should be the case; I do not think it was ever the intention of the rules that interim Supply should be objected to on Thursday or Friday. Hon. gentlemen opposite did not observe the intention of the rule then, but no doubt they are very anxious about it now. While that is undoubtedly the case I do not say that the Government intend to abuse the advantage. It may be an excellent thing to have a giant's strength but sometimes tyrannous to use it like a giant. Therefore, when the point comes up, as it will come up, in Supply, I do not think we will have any difficulty at all in arranging the matter satisfactorily. It is the intention of the Government to go into such Supply as has been already considered on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, as far as we possibly can. We will propose terms that will be fair and that I hope will be satisfactory to hon. gentlemen opposite.

The Minister of
Finance stated a moment ago that appointments to the Income Tax Service were not made through the Civil Service Commission. Will he now state how these officers are appointed?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All appointments to that service are made by the department.
I understood the minister to say they are made by the department, but must the appointments be recommended to the minister?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The appointments are all made on the recommendation of the chief officers of the department. It is a new service and we do not know exactly how far we may have to go, and whether it may be looked upon as permanent. However, we are working up a permanent organization that we hope will prove efficient.
The minister stated that recommendations for appointments were sent in to the chief officers of the department. If a member of the House makes a recommendation can it be accepted by the department?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no
doubt that not only can such a recommendation be received but that it will receive every fair, proper and due consideration.

The minister stated that the collection of income taxes amounted last year to $17,000,000, and that up to

March last the collections were $38,000,000. Will he be good enough to say what was the cost of making the collections for last year and this year?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The vote last year amounted to $1,200,000. This year the request is for $2,000,000. I am sorry to say I think there will have to be a supplementary vote to last year's amount.
But $2,000,000 is the total amount for this year?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
What is the amount of the income tax'collected in the different cities of Canada this year?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend that information at the moment, although I think that several returns dealing with the subject have already been tabled. I do not know whether my hon. friend's question has been asked before, but I will be very pleased to get the information for him if at all possible.

I would like to get also the amount of income tax paid in the city of Quebec. I am particularly interested in learning what it is.
Upon Mr. Rinfret and Mr. Gould rising at the same moment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to my hon. friend from St. James that the Chairman in recognizing speakers must alternate between the different sides.
I shall be pleased to give way to my hon. friend from Assiniboia.

Following a thought suggested to me by remarks from the hon member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) I would ask the minister if he does not think it would be a good idea if an officer were appointed in each of the rural municipalities for the purpose of collecting the income tax and compiling the records. I believe the farmers would be favourable to the appointment of an officer in each municipality to whom they could make their returns. I should also like to ask the minister, following up a question that was asked last year, if any arrangement has been entered into whereby individuals living in Great Britain and receiving incomes from Canada shall pay income tax to this country?

I had wished to put a question to the Minister of Marine but I see that he has now left the chamber. Per-
Haps the Minister of Finance can give me the information I want. I see on page 48 of the Estimates this item:
Naval Service-to provide for the maintenance of the Royal Canadian Navy, $2,500,000.
As compared with 1920-21 there is an increase of $500,000 in this vote. Last year we were told by the Minister of Marine that the cruisers had come from the British Admiralty in the nature of a gift which we could not very well refuse, but that $2,000,000 would be sufficient for their upkeep. Possibly before we vote one-sixth of this increase the Minister of Finance will tell us why the extra half million dollars is needed.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The original amount requested by the department last year was exactly what we find it in the vote this year. The reason why it was struck down to $2,000,000 in the 1920-21 Estimates was that a considerable portion of the year had elapsed before any expense was incurred.
I suppose we must feel satisfied with this answer on the interim Bill. We will discuss it more fully when we take up the item on the Estimates.
I would ask the minister for an answer to my question.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am getting up to answer my hon. friend. The whole question of income tax as between different countries is very difficult to determine. Of course, on the one hand it would seem that the country from which the income was earned, rather than the country in which it was spent, ought to be looked upon as the country to get the tax; but, on the other hand, if that principle were adopted great difficulties would ensue. For example, in England, where many people get all their income from outside investments, there would be a very great shortening of taxes collectible there, which is something the British Government could not entertain. So far as we are concerned in Canada, we have been doing our best to get a satisfactory solution of that difficulty. We may be able to get it, but I have some doubts. We are always willing to enter into any reciprocal arrangement.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, before this clause is carried I should like to know how this bonus is paid to the civil em-



ployees. I understand that there is a schedule in which employees are grouped according to salaries, the first group comprising those earning $1,000, the second, $2,000, the third $4,000, and so on. Are those receiving $5,000, $6,000 or even $10,000 receiving a bonus? I may say at once that I am altogether opposed to the payment of any bonus, because the cost of living has diminished very greatly since last year, and the bonus has been granted for the last three years on account of the high cost of living. It seems to me that if any bonus is granted it should be to the married men, and I would limit the bonus to those receiving not more than $2,000. As you are aware, Mr. Chairman, hundreds of thousands of our working men are idle to-day, and during the winter the federal, provincial and municipal authorities had to grant assistance to relieve their distress. In view of that, why should we continue paying a bonus to our civil servants? I wonder if the directors of a company that had lost, say, half a million dollars on the year's business would give a bonus to their employees. I do not think they would. This Government, I understand, has not done a very good business for the people for the year ended March 31, last. If so, I think the time has arrived when we should cut down expenses. This amount of $9,375,000 is pretty nearly one-fourth of the expenditure of the whole country in 1896. I remember, when I was a young man attending Ottawa University, I used to visit this House Thursday evenings, and on many occasions I heard lengthy discussions over item of $200 or $300. But to-day we think nothing of a million-dollar item. We must go back to the frame of mind of the old days and be more careful over our national expenditure.
It has been declared in the House on many occasions that the Civil Service in Ottawa is overmanned, and I know it to be the case. That being so, I cannot understand why the Civil Service Commission practically all the year round is sending out long lists of positions calling for new employees. I would suggest to the Government that the minister should know six months or a year in advance if more employees are called for in any department and he should satisfy himself that the additional employees are really needed. If an employee of the Public Works Department is not suitable for work in any other department, why should not the Government, which is paying that employee without getting any service in return, send him

to school in order that he may be prepared for service in another department? Why not do that instead of calling from time to time for new employees? I have talked the matter over with employees here in Ottawa, and they have felt compelled to accept my views. Many of them told me that they did not work more than five hours a day. I am sure that the civil employees do not work more than four or five hours a day, but they want big pay. If the service were not overmanned the employees would be better paid and the country would get better service. But where there are three or four employees to do one particular job, they depend upon each other to do it; they are all agreed that they should not work much, so the day passes without the work being done. The people are tired of paying taxes to maintain this army of civil employees. I wonder if a business man or a farmer could go on for ten or twenty years with his men working only four or five hours a day. No one could run his business under those conditions. The same is true of the manufacturer, of the merchant, of everybody engaged in any line of business. I am a man of economy, and I want to practise economy. I met on St. James street, in Montreal, some two or three weeks ago( a government employee who is living in that city and who was at one time a member of this House. The Prime Minister has just announced that the bonus would be reduced by 25 per cent, and he asked me if members of the House would be prepared to have their salaries reduced accordingly. My reply was that I received no benefit from the increase in the sessional [DOT] indemnity because I gave it to my people. So I said to him: You may go back to Ottawa once more and tell your old friends what to do; it is not up to me to do it. So I hope the Minister of Finance will give me the details I have asked for, that is, what men of different salaries receive from the bonus-those receiving $1,000,	$2,000,
$3,000 and $4,000. I notice in the third volume of the Auditor General's Report that in some cases caretakers of public buildings whose salary is $300 a year have been receiving a bonus of $420. In some cases the salary is less but the bonus is always $420. When the bonus is abolished for good,
I wonder how you will work it out that these men will be willing to remain in the service after receiving a bonus larger than their salary.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall have great pleasure in getting the details for my hon. friend and in giving them to him when the main vote is under consideration.

The bonus is being administered by the Civil Service Commission, very largely on the lines jndicated by the hon. member as correct lines. The amount of bonus paid is in inverse ratio to the salary; the smaller the salary the larger the bonus. There is also a differentiation between married and unmarried persons, in favour of those who are married. As the salary increases the bonus decreases, so that, as I recollect it, when the salary is over $3,000 the bonus ceases. But I shall have pleasure in giving my hon. friend the exact details at the proper time.
I understand, then, that in the case of a married man receiving $1,200 and a single man receiving the same salary, the single man will not get the same bonus as the married man?

The minister has just
made a statement which indicates the cause of much dissatisfaction and unrest among the mail carriers. He has said that the smaller the salary, the larger is the bonus. Well, that is the trouble with the bonus system and that is why the letter carriers throughout Canada are asking the Government to give them a stipulated salary so that they may be able to know what they are going to receive from time to time for the services they render. Necessarily, when a twenty-five per cent reduction is made in the bonus the man receiving the humble salary gets the small end of the deal. The system should be mapped out in such a way as to provide for the services rendered by the letter carriers of this country. During the war these men rendered splendid service without complaint. A large number of these positions have since the war been filled by returned soldiers, and it does seem unfair that the man with the smaller salary should have the biggest slice taken off his bonus. On page 80 of the Estimates I find that of the eighty odd employees of the Department of the Interior who are receiving salaries ranging from $2,500 to $4,000, sixty are getting substantial increases which will have the effect of compensating for the reduction of bonus. On page 81 we find that the men who are rendering real service in the humble capacities and receiving salaries of $1,000 and $1,020, are getting no increases. We should try to deal fairly with the men in humble circumstances, men who have families to maintain, and to educate, homes to buy and all the necessities of their families to provide for. We have in the city of Chatham, in my riding, a class of men on
the letter carriers' staff who are equal to any class of men in the Government service either in Ottawa or in any other part of the country. These men have already started out to provide themselves with homes, figuring that they would receive this bonus, and at this particular time, when they are on the point of having to meet their obligations, they are told that a cut of 25 per cent is to be made in the bonus, and they have no other way of providing money with which to meet their obligations. I am particularly anxious to impress up the minister the necessity of giving men in the humbler positions in the employ of the Government a stipulated salary, so that they may know what they have to depend upon receiving and that they may not have to depend upon a bonus such as they have at present.

I would
like to associate myself right now with my hon. friend (Mr. McCoig). To my mind the principle of bonus is absolutely wrong. It is not fair, just, nor right to expect any married man or any man who is conducting a business, to carry along on a system of bonus. There is nothing sane or safe or solid about such a system. Such a man does not know at what minute the bonus is going to be cut off. During war time it was quite justifiable that a bonus should be given; I am not raising any question about that part of it; I am speaking of the principle of bonus. Supposing a married man is getting a salary, we will say of $2,000 a year, and he is given a bonus of $300. He starts on this principle of living and he adds the $300 to his salary. The $300 is cut off automatically at some time, and he does not know when it is going to be cut off. Where does he land? I agree entirely with my hon. friend that the principle of bonus is absolutely wrong. If a man can earn $1,000 give him $1,000; if a man can earn $1,500, give him $1,500; but do not give it to him by way of a bonus.

Is it
the intention of the Government to reduce the bonus from time to time until it disappears?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps the
best way of answering the question is this. The reason why the bonus was put on was a reason which appealed to Parliament just as much as it appealed to most business houses during the period of the war. We had a high advancing cost of living, and it was felt that it was not on a permanent basis and that, therefore, instead of salaries

being increased beyond what was looked upon as a real economic value of the service, the proper thing to do was to give a bonus for the purpose of assisting employees over a period of high living costs. We are told that the cost of living is coming down, and the figures which have been submitted to the Government indicate that to be the fact, and they further indicate it to be the fact that having regard to the essential purpose for which the bonus was given, namely an increasing cost in living, it would be proper and just to make this year a reduction of 25 per cent in the amount of the bonus. That principle is the one which we have adopted, and I have! no doubt that principle is the one that ought to be adopted.

The
minister has not altogether answered my question. I want to know what the policy of the Government is regarding this bonus. Is it the policy of the Government to go on reducing the bonus, or to leave it as it is as long as they can afford to pay it?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Our policy- is to reduce it as the necessity for it disappears. It may be that the cost of living will be up next year, or it may be very much down. We all hope that it will be down. But the concrete action which ought to be taken is one which should be taken in view of the circumstances which may then develop. In addition to that, the Civil Service Commission, I think, are paying attention to points raised by hon. gentlemen who have previously spoken, and they are re-classifying and, in some instances, raising salaries, having regard to the value of the services given. Undoubtedly a bonus system ought to be a temporary system, and undoubtedly in time it ought to disappear, because, when a permanent higher standard of living is adopted, the value of the services having increased in regard to the economic situation, the bonus ought to disappear and its place be taken by a permanent salary.

I approve of the bonus system. It has been followed very largely by commercial firms, first, on account of the very great increase in the cost of living, and second, because it enabled

that increased cost to be met without upsetting the wage schedule. I suppose another reason for granting a bonus instead of an increase in salary was that it was easier to withdraw the bonus than to reduce the wages.
I think the Government should be very careful that they do not reduce the bonus too soon. I do not know that the cost of living has dropped so very much. I have made inquiry in the city of Ottawa and I find that the cost of bread rose during the war six cents above the normal price. That was the top price. And to-day bread is only one cent below that peak figure, in spite of the fact that wheat has dropped from $3.25 to $1.65. I am informed that about thirty per cent of our civil servants receive an annual salary of about $800. If that is the fact, certainly they are not overpaid, and the wonder to me is how they can live on $800 a year. I would again ask the Government to be very careful not to reduce the bonus too soon. I think the Government is to be congratulated for having followed the bonus system, which has been adopted by nearly all commercial houses.

I quite agree with what has been said as to the bonus system. I do not believe it should have been adopted, but inasmuch as' the Government has adopted that system, I do not think the time is opportune for making a cut in the bonus. We all realize from reading the press and the government reports that there has been some drop in the cost of living, but to the ordinary man receiving a salary of from $1,500 to $2,000 a year, that drop in prices is not appreciable. Take the case of the postmen in the city of Windsor, for instance, and other civil servants. They cannot possibly get a decent house at less than $35 or $40 a month rent. Then, last year they were paying from $20 to $25 a ton for coal. That means they would be spending $30 a month on coal, burning a ton and a half a month. So on those two items alone $70 is gone without a dollar for clothing, without a dollar for food, without a dollar for the doctor and many other expenses that a married man with a family necessarily has to meet. I repeat, I am opposed to the bonus system, but I believe the time is not opportune for making a cut in the bonus. I believe that the men should pe paid a decent living salary, which they could be assured of for some time to come, and make their arrangements accordingly. In that way only will you get good service. Naturally the men are unsettled to-day, when they do not know from day to day just what they are going to receive. It is not reasonable treatment for the Government to mete out to its employees. It is not the treatment that would be accorded by private concerns, and we should at least put ourselves in that class with respect to our employees. Let us give the men a decent living wage so that they can bring up their families properly.

I do not want to prolong the discussion. I am against the bonus system, but I think there should be no cut at the present time. I believe that the men should be paid a living wage, so that they would know from month to month and year to year what they were going to receive and be able to make their arrangements accordingly. I am decidedly against cutting the bonus at the present time. Although the price of some things may have come down to some extent, the cost of living is not appreciably less than it was a considerable time ago. Many of our postmen with a large family get just enough to keep body and soul together when you include the bonus, and to make a cut in the bonus now certainly seems to me to be inopportune. In my own town I know that some of them have had to do outside work after hours in order to make both ends meet. The salaries they receive to-day, I understand, are a minimum of $900 and a maximum of $1,200. I think if we put ourselves in their shoes for a moment we should appreciate how difficult it is for a man with a family of four or five children to bring them up as they should be brought up on such a small salary. The salary is small enough as it is, and to make a cut in the bonus is only making matters so much worse. My idea is that there ought to be a living wage paid. I think you would then get more loyal service. The civil servants would endeavour to give their best in the positions they hold.

I have been particularly impressed with what hon. gentlemen have said regarding the case of the postmen. That is one service which it seems to me requires the particular attention of the Government. Most of these men have seen service overesas, where they received very small remuneration, and in their present position in the service to-day they are receiving very meagre pay. Tile work is very arduous; the men have to travel back and forth on the pavements, and in consequence of their employment in all kinds

of weather they are liable to rheumatism and other ailments. You might say they are almost continuously employed night and day. The cost of living in some of the smaller cities has not appreciably decreased. Before the bonus was granted, it certainly had increased, and I do not believe it has decreased sufficiently to warrant the minister in cutting the bonus to the extent of 25 per cent. Coal and rent are two main items in the cost of living, and these are as high, if not higher, than they ever were. I would urge the Government to continue the bonus without any cut for this year at least, and then perhaps next year there would not be so much ground for complaint at a cut, providing the cost of living had decreased as we anticipate it will. This is one service which I think should receive the sympathetic support of the Government. These men are working in all kinds of weather, and they, are meagrely paid. I think the Government should see that they receive such remuneration as will enable them to maintain at least their present standard of living.
Does this bonus apply to the superannuated officers of the Government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
Is it the intention of the Government to supplement the retiring allowance of those who have been superannuated? I know there has been a petition circulated to that effect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There was a question put to the Government on the matter, and it was answered to-day.
Does my hon. friend remember the answer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was that the bonus does not apply to them, and that the Government under the Act of 1920 provided certain pensions for pensioners in England-that was part of the question-but had not decided to have that apply in Canada.

lam heartily in accord with what has been said in favour of the postmen. I am certainly not in favour of a cut in the bonus at the present time. These men are performing one of the most important services, and their salaries are very small. The minimum is $900 and the maximum $1,200, I understand. While there might have been some slight decrease in the cost of living, the main items, fuel and rent, have certainly not gone down,
[Mr. Gordon.1
and I therefore think it would be inopportune to make a cut in the bonus at the present time. I concur in what has been said opposing its reduction.

On principle, I oppose the payment of a bonus, because I consider that civil servants should be given salaries sufficient to enable them to live in reasonable comfort; and, in the meantime, I understand that the Civil Service Commission is trying to bring about an equitable adjustment of this matter. As things are, however, I do not think that the bonus at present paid civil servants throughout the country should be reduced. While it is true that the prices of one or two commodities have gone down a little, no one can deny that on the whole the cost of living is pretty much on the same level as it was last year, and certainly rents in the cities are, if anything, on the increase. Under the circumstance, therefore, a reduction in the bonus at this time would be unjust. I would suggest to the Government, that, at any rate, no civil servant receiving less than $2,000 should suffer a reduction in the bonus paid him last year. We all know that to-day a family man in receipt of even $2,000 finds it extremely difficult to make ends meet, and those receiving less than this sum cannot afford to have the little bonus paid them reduced, as can men receiving $4,000 and $5,000 a year.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I only wish to urge the Government, in a very few words, not to reduce the bonus which the civil servants have been granted for a couple of years, because, to my mind, we do not live at a time when such a question should be considered. As far as I am concerned, I sincerely sympathize with all the civil employees, and particularly so with those of the capital or of the city where I have the honour to reside. Having increased the judges' salaries as well as our own parliamentary indemnity, we should not think of reducing the salaries of those poor employees. The salary received by and the bonus granted to each of them are hardly sufficient to ensure a decent living, and I know a good many whose home has been visited by want. No, the cost of living has not decreased, I should rather think it has increased. I read with pleasure a few days ago in the press that one of the leaders of industry in our district, surnamed the Lumber King, had decided to increase the salaries of his men on account of the high cost of living. It seems

to me that by cutting down the bonus to the extent of 25 per cent, the Government is doing something that is not at all justified and I dare hope they will reverse their decision.
During the discussions that took place this week I had occasion to express my opinion on the question. I think the Government ought to pay the entire bonus and even increase it in some cases. I concur in the opinion of the hon. members who have said that it was a vicious principle to grant a bonus to public employees and that they should rather increase their salaries. I have already stated that we were not justified at this time in reducing that bonus after having paid it for one, two or three years, and that justice demands to-day that the entire salary and bonus be paid. Many employees have been in the public service for a number of years and they are in hopes of receiving a sufficient salary to provide for their families. I am pleased now to act as their interpreter and champion. I am in no way interested and I must say that during my public career such advice as I gave to those wishing to enter the public service has always been of such a nature as to dissuade them. I told them: "My good friends, do not enter public service."
In concluding, I beg to say once more that public servants have the right to expect a fair and just treatment. It is not' given to every one of them to have interpreters within the hearing of the Government; a great number of them are mechanics and their surroundings are perhaps unknown to our ministers; these people are not permitted to knock at the doors of those gentlemen in order to make known their circumstances and to voice their just claims. I am pleased, as I have said, to represent them and say to the Government on their behalf that the bonus should be increased instead of being reduced. I think that this is a step the Government ought to take.
Did the employees of the Quebec arsenal receive their bonus last year and this year, as far as it has gone? Will the Minister of Militia give me an answer?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is not strictly relevant to the clause under consideration, but the hon. member may ask it by unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The hon. member asked me the question a moment ago and I said I would get the information and give it to him. I have not yet got it, but -when it is available he shall have it.

I would ask the Prime Minister to consider the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Turgeon), that salaries not exceeding $2,000 shall be exempt from the reduction this year. This suggestion deserves the best consideration of the Government. No man in this country to-day who has a family can decently exist on less than this amount, and as members of Parliament, I do not think we should go on record as asking people to live on less than a living wage, and I think that taking off twenty-five per cent from the bonus in the case of men who are receiving less than $2,000 a year -well I would not like to characterize it too strongly, but it would seem to be nothing short of an outrage.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
language is pretty strong.
I do not think it is too strong.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not doubt the sincerity of the hon. member at all, nor indeed of any hon. member, in his remarks as to this bonus question. But it must be recalled that the duty of the Government is one thing, and the privilege of the Opposition is another. It is one of the great privileges of members of an Opposition to complain that each and every vote is not large enough but that the total is too large. The problem that confronts the Government is to keep the total down and to get the items increased. We had no idea in the world that a reduction of the bonus would be popular anywhere. Such a thing is inconceivable, it is undoubtedly unpopular in the Service, and undoubtedly unpopular among the friends of the Service. But the question the Government had to consider was: What is the right thing to do?-and we had to do the right thing, no matter what it entailed. First of all let me point this out. The official figures show that there has been a reduction-I think approximately of fifteen per cent-in the cost of living. I know that is disputed. I know you could dispute over it for hours and not get very far, but the official figures show it. We do not reduce the salary of anybody twenty-five per cent, but only reduce the bonus that he gets by that amount, and that I understand averages only about five per cent of the salary received. Consequently there is only a five per cent reduction of salary as against a fifteen per cent reduction in the cost of living. Now it is only fair to say that at the time the bonus was fixed the cost of living had

not got to the maximum-it reached it somewhat later-and that this fifteen per cent reduction or something like that has occurred since the maximum in the cost of living was reached, not since the time the bonus was fixed. But as against that there is this consideration, that the scale of salaries which has been adopted by the commission was arrived at in this way, and it is of the utmost importance that it be understood: There was a gradual increase in the cost of living for some years before the war. A certain number of years were taken and the line indicating the cost of living runs through that number of years. In determining the figures for the new classification, or the new scale of salaries, the Civil Service Commission simply projected that ascending line through the years of the war thereby giving increases very substantially, in addition to the bonus, or cost of living increase, which was granted. Therefore on the completion of the reclassification very decided advances took place as well as advances not in effect previously
that is to say advances that correspond to increases in the cost of living while now the cost of living is actually declining. All that had to be taken into account. It was taken into account, and the Government really thought that it was acting on the side of fairness, if not a little better, in its decision on this question, having regard to the imperative need of economy in the public service.
Now the fact must also be taken into account that the cost of the public service
and if that question is raised I earnestly hope my words will not raise it because we are anxious to get on-the cost of the public service, by reason of the increase in classification and of the bonus, and eliminating entirely increases in the service- and indeed there have been very great increases has gone up at least between one hundred and two hundred per cent. Taking account of absolutely necessary increases since 1914 I think the figures have risen I speak now from memory-from about $28,000,000 to over $65,000,000. The diminution that is provided for here takes off but $3,200,000 for one year, providing that the diminution applies throughout the year and to it alone.
This also must be taken into account -the condition of labour generally throughout the country. It is unfair, wholly unfair, on the part of the Government to pay any class of labour substantially above what that class can obtain elsewhere, because if that is done the outside man en-
gaged at lower pay in a similar class of work is forced to contribute to the man that happens to be in the Government service something that the former needs more than the latter-the outside man is taxed to pay the extra amount the man in the Government service receives, which undoubtedly is not fair. Consequently we felt that because of the conditions obtaining now in the industrial world generally, as well as for the other reasons I have mentioned, this very small reduction should be made in the bonus. Now, if every man who receives less than $2,000 should still receive what he got before, is not the very injustice I have represented going to be ' perpetuated? Undoubtedly it is. It is true, it is hard getting along when the salary is under that sum, but it is also true that thousands and tens of thousands-yes, hundreds of thousands, if not millions-do get along in this country on a salary under that amount, and at the same time have to contribute to the payment of these very people whose cause is advocated here. I could name to my hon. friend from North Essex many and many a family, not in receipt of any revenue from the Government of Canada, who are getting on with a good deal less than that amount at this time, and when the hon. member makes his plea let him remember he is asking that these people outside, who are already receiving less salary and perhaps doing more work, to contribute to make still greater the advantage of those who happen to be in the public service. It must also be recalled that in the public service the hours are pretty good, and while there are many excellent public servants-and many, I have not the least doubt, who are doing more than they are getting paid for-what is inevitable in all public services results: the need of uniformity is such that you are bound to be overpaying many, and at the same time underpaying a few; that is an incident of public service, no matter where it is. So that, having in view the conditions of work, the hours of labour, the certainty of employment, having in view corresponding conditions in the industrial world generally, I do not think there is cause of complaint as to any part of the public service, that is to say, nothing in the way of general cause for complaint.

I congratulate the
Prime Minister upon the stand he has taken. Let me state further many instances in the city of Ottawa three or four members of the same family are working in

the Civil Service. I do not see why four persons of the same family in one house should receive four bonuses. When I first addressed the committee this afternoon I was speaking about the Inside Service here. The Outside Service I know is not so well paid and includes the men engaged in the delivery of the mails all over the country. But in Ottawa every one in the Inside Service is well paid, and during my seventeen years as a member of the House I have been asked by hundreds of my people to try to get them a job in the service here. Ten years ago any of them would only be too willing to receive a salary of $100 per month for a short working day of five hours,, for they could not get anything like that remuneration down in my country, or in Montreal or anywhere else. I say again that the workingmen who are idle to-day are not ready to pay bonuses to those who have a well-paid job the year round.

I approve of what the
right hon. Prime Minister said, and I should like him to even up things. There is a class of men in the Outside Service who are certainly underpaid; I refer to the rural mail carriers throughout the country. We have in the Inside Service some employees who get large salaries and a bonus in addition. I would advise him to cut the bonus of those employees who are getting over $2,000 by fifty per cent, and apply the saving towards a bonus to the rural mail carriers.

Were not the bonuses
graded according to salary?-that is to say, higher bonuses were given to those receiving the smaller salaries? If that is right, then my hon, friend would not be logical in making the cut apply only to those getting over $2,000.	.

I think my hon. friend
from Frontenac is wrong. I do not think this bonus applies to the rural mail carriers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He is right; the larger bonus is given to the lower-paid employees.

But are the rural mail
carriers included among those who get bonuses?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not those who have
contracts. They are not in the service at all, they are contractors.
But they are underpaid. They take the contracts at a low figure because the department will not allow more than a certain figure per mile.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chairman certainly cannot allow a discussion respecting the contracts of rural mail carriers. It would be absolutely out of order on this item and might be prolonged indefinitely.

I would advise the Prime Minister to leave the bonus cut for those receiving a salary of less than $2,000 at 25 pfer cent and reduce the bonus of those receiving over $2,000 by fifty per cent. Then we will have some money to provide for the rural mail carriers.

In vie\y of the representations that have been made by various hon. members I would ask the Prime Minister whether he would consider abolishing the bonus system and putting the employees on a straight salary basis.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That undoubtedly is
the intention. The bonus system was instituted to take care of what it was hoped would be a temporary condition. That condition is now in process of disappearance, and as it disappears it is the intention that the bonus that accompanied it shall likewise disappear, and that the Civil Service shall return to a straight salary basis.

Is this cut of 25 per cent
the forerunner of similar cuts at stated intervals?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That will all depend
upon the disappearance of the temporary cause, that is, the abnormal cost of living due to the war. As rapidly as that recedes it is intended that the bonus shall be reduced. Consequently we cannot say what the next reduction will be or when it will be made. I suppose in the event of another war we might have to increase instead of decrease the bonus.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-account to be rendered in detail.
