speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Will the
moneys appropriated under this Act be surrounded by the same conditions as surround interim Supply when reached by agreement; in other words, will the moneys be used only for what is absolutely necessary until all the Supply is voted?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The ordinary conditions of the vote on interim Supply will be observed.

I would direct the attention
of the Prime Minister to the provision that a detailed statement shall be submitted to

the House within fifteen days of the next session. Having in mind our experience this year, of delay in bringing down the Auditor General's report and consequently the impossibility of the Public Accounts Committee meeting, will the Prime Minister see that the Finance Department gives closer attention to its duties next year so that the Auditor General's report will be presented according to statute?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid I will have to give a negative answer to my hon. friend, for two reasons: First, because there was nothing unusual," unless it was unusual speed, in the production of the Auditor General's Report this year; and second, because I do not think it is possible for the Finance Department to urge these things along faster than they do. I have had occasion to examine the matter, and I assure my hon. friend that no stone is left unturned in trying to observe the law. I sometimes think it is unwise to have the law remain as it is in that regard, because it becomes impossible to observe it, and it has been traditionally so. But X will give my hon. friend an undertaking that the utmost that can be done will be done to have the law observed just as closely as is practicable.

In view of the diminishing strength of the Government, I think that the question should hardly be pressed upon my right hon. friend as to what will be done next year. At that time he is scarcely likely to be performing his present duties.'

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Right Hon. Sir George Foster (Minister of Trade and Commerce) the House went into Committee of the Whole on the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
That it is expedient to provide that the creation of the Canadian Wheat Board hy the Governor in Council under the provisions of the Order in Council of the thirty-first day of July, one thousand nine hundred and nineteen (F.C. 1589), the appointments made thereunder and the powers, duties and rights of the said Board and of the Executive Committee, Chairman and members of the said Board as set forth in the said Order in Council and in the Orders in Council of the seventh day of August, one thousand nine hundred and nienteen (P.C. 1659), the twenty-ninth day of August, one thousand nine hundred and nineteen (P.C.	1817), the
eighteenth day of October, one thousand nine 
hundred and nineteen (P.C. 2148), the third day of December, one thousand nine hundred and nineteen (P.C. 2430), the ninth day of December, one thousand nine hundred and nineteen (P.C. 2462), and in two Orders in Council of the eighteenth day of August, one thousand nine hundred and nineteen (P.C. 1741 and P.C. 1762), and in any other Orders in Council passed with reference to the said Board, and the rules, regulations and orders made by the said Board, be ratified and confirmed as on and from the respective dates of the said Orders in Councils, rules and regulations; and that the powers, duties and rights of the said Board, the Executive Committee, the Chairman and members, be continued in full force and effect so far as it may be necessary and convenient for winding up and concluding the unsettled business of the Wheat Board, or any business arising therefrom ; and that the Governor in Council shall have power during the continuance of such business to fill any vacancy in the chairmanship or the membership thereof and to make any regulations he may deem necessary or convenient for conducting, managing and winding up the said business of the said Board.-The Minister of Trade and Commerce.

The press would indicate
that the minister is about to appoint another commission to investigate the grain trade in general. Will that commission have authority to dip into all the business of previous grain commissions which the minister had had under his department?

I do not think they would have any power to go into this, which was an independent commission and has carried out its work. It is not intended to give the new commission such powers as my hon. friend speaks of.

Is it not the case that all
the irregularities complained of, which are the grounds upon which the Government is appointing this further commission, occurred within the last year? For it is to be remembered that these grain commissions handled the grain business in Canada for two or three years.

Oh, no, the
Canadian Wheat Board simply had the duty of buying in the first place and disposing afterwards of the grain, during the time that they had power. But the work of the commission which is to be appointed will be a far wider work, involving questions connected with the whole machinery of delivery, storage, handling, transport and marketing of the grain in general.
How far back will it go?

I do not know.
I suppose they will not be limited in that respect; they will use their judgment as to how far back it is necessary to extend their examinations.
I understand that the Canadian Wheat Board are asking for winding-up powers?
Yes.
What amount of money, if any, is standing to the credit of the Canadian Wheat Board, and has the minister come to any conclusion as to what shall be done with it?

The object of
the Canadian Wheat Board, as my hon. friend knows, was, after marketing the grain, to get the price received therefor, less expenses, into the hands of the original producers of the grain. The amounts have all been distributed up to an average of $2.63 per bushel. I do not know what amount is on hand; it will depend on its size whether it is worth while attempting to distribute it among the original producers. If this is not done, some other provision will have to be made for it; probably it will go into the consolidated revenue fund. The amount may be so small that the cost of distributing it would be almost as great as the amount itself. We cannot decide that question until we ascertain in the final adjustment of the business just what surplus is on hand.

I understand
that the amount will likely be so small that it would not pay to give to each individual producer the small balance coming to him. But I am informed that in the aggregate it will be a considerable sum. I would like to make this suggestion to the minister. A blight known as the rust has been having an adverse effect upon the production of wheat in Western Canada. Would he consider the advisability of setting aside this sum-perhaps it would need to be supplemented-for the purposes of a thorough investigation with a view to finding means of scientifically combatting this rust pest, which is very seriously affecting the production of wheat?

I should suppose that is being done to a certain extent by the Department of Agriculture. If it is not being done by them to an extent commensurate with the menace of the pest, I suppose it would be the duty of the agriculture departments here and in the provinces to prosecute the work still further. To the extent that this work is carried on by the Department of Agriculture here the money must be provided out of the consolidated revenue fund, so that if the Canadian Wheat Board surplus goes into that fund it
would in the end be paid out through the appropriate department for the purpose suggested by my hon. friend. However, his suggestion is well worthy of being taken into account.

I urge the minister to give the committee a definite promise that he will see to it that a special effort will be made to combat this rust pest and that it will not be left entirely to the Department of Agriculture.

I could not
give my hon. friend any such assurance as that, but I will collogue with my colleague the Minister of Agriculture in reference to the suggestion.

I promise the
minister that I will remind him of this later.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Sir GEORGE FOSTER thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 75, concerning the Canadian Wheat Board.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) does not appear to be present, and I think some other hon. members on this side would like to be present when this Bill comes up. Why not leave it over until after recess?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Minister of Justice will not be present after recess and it is important that this Bill have attention now. I could give the reasons, but that is not necessary. The only consideration was this, whether the $5,000 that had been received as administrator was taxable, and we are prepared to take that up now. I do not see any reason for delay.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is all right.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-section 11 of chapter 56 of statutes of 1920 not to apply to present Chief Justice, as the emoluments of his office were not increased by that Act.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
This is the clause that will have to be amended. When the Bill was before the House on a former occasion, exception was taken to the clause as it now stands, because it would exempt from taxation, not only the $10,000 which the Chief Justice has heretofore received, but also his $5,000 allowance as administrator. An amendment has therefore been prepared by the Minister of Justice which ~ he has placed in my hands as he is not able to be present this evening. This amendment is to overcome that difficulty by providing that the $5,000 which the Chief Justice receives as administrator shall be taxable, but that the $10,000 shall always continue to be exempt. The amendment which I move reads:
That the words "so much of the annual salary of" be inserted in line 6 after the words applied to," and that the words "as amounts to $10,000" he inserted in line 8 after the words "of Canada."
That will make the section read:
1. Section 11 of chapter 56 of the Statues of 1920, entitled an Act to amend the Judges' Act, shall not apply nor be deemed to have applied to so much of the annual salary of the Right Honourable Sir Louis H. Davies. K.C.M.G., the present Chief Justice of Canada as amounts to $10,000.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Had Sir
Louis Davies any understanding with the Government, as to what part of his salary if any, would be exempt?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I understand there was no arrangement. I do not think the matter was even discussed.
Does a similar exemption apply to all the judges in Canada?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: They are exempt, bur not in respect of increases which were made last session. When their salaries were increased, the increases were made subject: to taxation.
The original salaries were exempt?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Were they exempted at the time the judges were appointed, or were they exempted by the Act introduced by the Minister of Finance when income taxes were introduced into Canada?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think they have always been exempted under the clauses of the Judges' Act. ,

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 3-when judges not to be paid travelling expenses.
What is the necessity for this clause?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think only in Ontario is any local residence required of judges. By the statutes of Ontario a judge of the High Court must reside at the city of Toronto. As a matter of practice, a judge ought to reside at the chief town of the province where the court is held; but in many provinces we find that a judge resides, hot where the chief courts are held and where he performs his daily functions, but at a point more or less remote. And the practice in the past has been that a judge will charge his travelling expenses in going daily to the place where he holds his court. The object of the present clause is that a judge shall not be entitled to charge travelling expenses in going to the place where he holds court. If he desires to live outside of the capital city of the province or the place where the courts are usually held, he shall travel at his own expense. In British Columbia he must reside at one of two places, either at Vancouver or at Victoria. In the other provinces I think there is a single place designated as the chief place for holding of these courts, and in going to and returning from that place, a judge shall not charge travelling expenses.
As regards Saskatchewan, if a judge chooses to reside in Saskatoon, he gets no travelling allowance for going down to the city of Regina where courts have to be held?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is right.
Am I to understand that as regards Prince Edward Island, a judge will not receive travelling expenses when he goes to hold court in Summerside and Georgetown, outside of the city of Charlottetown?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is a circuit court; that is a different thing.
The Supreme Court?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
A judge of the Supreme Court going on circuit gets his travelling expenses. It is only for courts or chambers

held in Charlottetown that he shall not charge travelling expenses. He should live there.

As regards New Brunswick, under our Act judges have to hold chambers on certain days of the week at Fredericton, St. John and Moncton. The judge has to go from St. John to Moncton. Under the Act will he not be allowed travelling expenses?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Tlje section is very
plain on that:
w
in the province of New Brunswick no judge of the Supreme Court shall receive any travelling allowance for courts or chambers held at either one of the cities of Fredericton or St. John unless he resides at the other of the said cities or in the immediate vicinity thereof.

I would suggest that Moncton should be added there, because the judges are obliged to hold chambers in the city of Moncton just as well as in Fredericton and St. John. If a judge lives at Fredericton and has to hold chambers at St. John, he is allowed travelling expenses, or if he lives at St. John and has to hold chambers at Fredericton, he is allowed travelling expenses. I think if a judge in St. John or Fredericton has to hold chambers in Moncton, he also should be allowed travelling expenses.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Is Moncton established as a place to hold chambers by some provincial law?
Yes.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Then I think it should be added.

I know they hold chambers there, hut before I say it is established by law, I should like to look up the Act. I can let the minister know definitely at eight o'clock when we resume.
At Six o'clock, the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at Eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were considering Bill No. 60 to amend the Judges' Act. Clauses 1 and 2 had been adopted; clause 3 was under consideration. Shall clause 3 carry?

During the dinner hour I had an opportunity of conferring with the minister (Mr. Guthrie), and apparently we
do not understand each other in regard to the objection I raised to this section. The point is that one of the judges of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick resides at Moncton, one of the larger cities of the province, where the legal business is as great as that at either St. John or Fredericton, if not greater; but when this judge holds court at St. John or Fredericton, he receives no travelling expenses, although other judges, travelling between these two points, are indemnified. Judge Chandler chose to reside at Moncton because it is within easy access to the whole north shore of the province, being in proximity to Res-tigouche, Gloucester, Northumberland, and Westmoreland. It does not seem fair to me that he should be compelled to change his residence from Moncton to St. John or Fredericton, or in the alternative be penalized by having to pay his own travelling expenses when doing chamber work in either of these two places. A resident judge of Fredericton or St. John, when going to Moncton, is paid travelling expenses. If this is a policy of the Government, I can, of course, do nothing, but I submit to my hon. friend that it is unjust to the judge who resides in Moncton.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: During adjournment I had the benefit of a brief interview with my hon. friend in regard to this clause. I should not like to create an exception with reference to New Brunswick or the city of Moncton. The object of the Bill is not to penalize or inconvenience any judge.
Well, that is the effect.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Nor is that the effect, in my humble judgment. We recognize that in certain provinces the capital is not the metropolitan centre nor the place where the chief business is done, and in some provinces we have therefore allowed two places to be named as the principal centres for the holding of courts. In British Columbia, Victoria happens to be the capital, but Vancouver is the larger centre, and there is more court business actually transacted there than in Victoria. Consequently, we have named two places in that province as central locations of court. In Alberta it happens that Calgary is larger than Edmonton, and in that province, again, we have allowed two places. In Saskatchewan there is only one; in Manitoba only one; in Ontario only one; in Quebec only one; in Nova Scotia only one and in Prince Edward Island only one.
Are you referring to the Appellate Court?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I am not referring to the circuit courts held by the judges who carry on ordinary assize business. Those judges will be paid in the future as in the past. The object is to reduce the amount the Government has to pay for travelling expenses. When a judge accepts the appointment he knows the conditions and should live in proximity to the court. In Ontario, he must by statute live in Toronto. Under this amendment we have given a good deal of liberty to the province of New Brunswick, providing that a judge may reside either at St. John, the larger city, or at Fredericton, the capital, where the appellate courts are held. If he lives at Fredericton and has to go to St. John he is allowed expenses, and he is also allowed travelling expenses when performing any judicial duties in any other part of the province. Judges, however, are not permitted to live in any part of the province they choose and charge up their travelling expenses when going to St. John or Fredericton, where they ought to reside. The object of the Bill is to limit the amount now paid by the country for travelling expenses to judges who do not see fit to reside in the proximity of the chief court. The proposal is a most reasonable one, and I do not care to make an exception in regard to New Brunswick.

The minister contends that this will effect a saving, but, as a matter of fact, it will not. He allows travelling expenses from Fredericton to St. John and vice versa, or from either of these places to Moncton. I do not see why he could not allow expenses from Moncton to there.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That judge could live in Fredericton or St. John.

He could by selling his property. It is a great convenience to the lawyers in all the counties on the north shore of the province to have a judge resident in Moncton, where a large amount of legal business is done, and I really do not see that the Government will save much money through this provision. I voice my protest against it as working a great injustice to the practising barristers, as well as to the litigants in that section of the province.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When shall the Bill be read the third time?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Now.
I do not think it should be read the third time to-night.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Next sitting of the House.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (for the Minister pf Justice), Bill No. 57, to amend the Post Office Act was read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-insuring mail matter.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence

speechtext: Is this an international regulation?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It is international to the extent that this is the law which now applies in Great Britain and in the United States. I am not able to say whether other countries in the Postal Union have adopted it.
In what company is the insurance carried?
Does the Government carry the insurance itself?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes, the Government charges a reasonable fee and carries the insurance itself.

What objection, if any, would there be to raising that minimum substantially? There may be some objec-

tion and I would be glad to know if there is, because it would be of decided convenience to the public, I should judge, if the minimum were placed at a higher figure than $100.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I understand that in
Great Britain, and also in the United States, the maximum is higher than $100. But the idea was that we would start with that maximum, try it out in actual operation for probably a year, and then, if the operation justified such a course, we might increase it. But we would like to try it out with this limitation in the meantime. I do not know what the limitation is in Great Britain and the United States but it is higher than $100.
Is there any company dealing with such matters at the present time?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There are a number of companies which insure valuable packages, either by post, express or by freight. For instance bonds transmitted through the mails, are, as. a rule, insured in recognized insurance companies.

The minister's remarks would indicate that there is a special branch of the Post Office Department under which this insurance is carried on. If that is the case who is in charge of such special branch?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
There is no such branch,
I am informed, in the Post Office Department.

How does the minister reconcile that statement with his previous statement that insurance was carried on in the department. If there is such a branch, I would ask what insurance company is carrying the insurance that the hon. gentleman has been talking about?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The post office insurance to-day is carried on under the section of the Post Office Act which I am asking the repeal of. There is at present a limitation in that section, the maximum value of parcels insurable is $25, and the usual fee of ten cents is charged for registration.
To whom does the premium go?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The premium, if that term be correct, derived from the sale of registration stamps goes to the Post Office Department.
To what company does it go after that?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It stays in the coffers of the Government of Canada, which bears the loss.

Does the department assure itself that the amount of money claimed has been put in the letter? Otherwise it is possible for frauds to occur. A man might get a letter insured for $100 and still not have that amount in the letter.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The door is always open for a certain amount of fraud, at the instance of evilly disposed persons, in regard to every matter of insurance. All that one can do is to take every reasonable precaution to prevent fraud, although I am satisfied that frauds in regard to insurance are committed from time to time the world over. The experience in this country is limited, of course, but we have not found that fraud is perpetrated in these matters, although it may have happened.
Does the department make any money out of this insurance proposition?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There is the ordinary ten cent fee charged for registration now, and as a result of that registration there is an insurance up to $25. Whether we have made any money out of insurance or not it is hard to say. The old registration rate was five cents.
The Deputy Postmaster General is present and he ought to know whether the department has m^de money out of that insurance or not.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Before the clause in question was adopted the experience in the Post Office Department was that there was a net loss on registered mail. I am informed that with the ten cent registration rate, and the limitation of $25 of insurance, the department thinks it is coming out about even or perhaps a little better than that.
That is not my question. I asked whether the insurance has brought a revenue to the department?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There has been no insurance in the past.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On Section 2-Letters posted unpaid or underpaid to go forward charged with double postage.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
This contemplates a change. The present system, as the committee is aware, is that where a letter is partially prepaid it is forwarded to its

destination and a double amount of postage is there collected from the recipient of that letter. Letters which are wholly unpaid are not forwarded to the address but go direct to the dead letter office. The system proposed under this clause is that letters wholly unpaid shall go forward to the person to whom they are addressed, and from that person shall be collected double the amount of the ordinary postage. I am informed that this is the system adopted by every country in the Postal Union save Canada. The experience in other countries has proved the worth of this proposal, and the Post Office Department here desires to adopt it. It has been suggested that the system will be open to some kind of manipulation whereby people out of revenge or spite, if they like, may send anybody unpaid mail matter and the recipient will be charged double postage but that has qot been the experience, I understand, in other countries. Another thing to be noted is that under the present Post Office law, letters without postage have to be sent to the dead letter office, and very frequently they do not contain the address of the sender. Under the present law we can charge the sender the amount of unpaid postage when the letter reaches the dead letter office; but so many communications are signed anonymously or with the word "father," "mother," "aunt," or "John," or "Henry" or the like that there is in reality no address and consequently a large amount of postage is annually lost. Under the system proposed by this clause the recipient will receive the letter and double postage will be demanded. The letter will only go to the dead letter office in the event of its refusel by the recipient.
Would the law compel the addressee to accept an unstamped letter?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not think there is any law to compel a person to accept a letter from the post office. If he does accept it he must pay double postage.

I am afraid the section as drafted leaves the matter somewhat in doubt. It says:
Letters addressed to any place in Canada on which the postage has not been prepaid or not sufficiently prepaid by the sender shall he forwarded to their desitnation charged with double the amount of the postage thereon-
Now, if the Government charges something against a citizen it seems to me there is an implication that the citizen is obliged to pay.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Not if he refuses delivery: "shall be collected on delivery."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-obligations to ferrymen:
What is meant by "ferryman" in this clause?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I suppose it is the usual interpretation of the word "ferryman"; that is, any man in charge of a small water craft plying between well known points.

Between the city of
Quebec and the Isle of Orleans, a distance of about six miles, there is a ferry service. For about a year past the man in charge of the mails on the island of Orleans has been using the ferry boat for his bags of mail without paying the ferry company anything for the privilege. Under the Liberal regime the Government used to pay for the carriage of those, mails on the ferry. Is this clause intended to meet a case of this sort? This section reads, "Every ferryman shall, upon request and without delay, convey over his ferry," etc. That leaves the Government plenty of scope to satisfy their friends. Moreover the section provides that "such service may be fixed by contract." It does not say that it shall be fixed by contract, again making it possible for the Government to protect their friends whenever they want to. "And shall in no case exceed what is ordinarily charged the public." I know of no case where the public is charged for carrying so many bags of mail as in this particular case. In the summer time the island of Orleans is one of the most attractive holiday resorts in the Dominion, and with the ferry boats filled with bags of mail, for which the company does not receive any consideration, the regular passenger accommodation is restricted.
I do not think it is right that a ferry company should be called upon to carry the mails free.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that this section is not drafted with regard to any case such as he has in mind. But there is an idea among the public that when working for the Government they should charge more than they would charge a private corporation or person. This clause enables the Government to have its mails carried on a ferry at the same rate as the public is charged, and if a horse and carriage with a quantity of mail has to be conveyed by ferry the charge will be just the same as that for the conveyance of ordinary freight. There is no

injury to any one. This section merely fixes a uniform rate for ferrymen throughout the Dominion, and it is to be the ordinary rate charged to the public.
Where will you draw the line? The city of Quebec is seven miles from the island of Orleans; would you call that distance a ferry?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.
If the distance was thirty miles would it be a ferry?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I would not draw any line. I think the word "ferry" has a well understood legal meaning.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the section repealed?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The section repealed provides for a system of arbitration as to prices and the like. It is very cumbersome and involved.
I do not want to let that go-	,

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The member for
Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) has tried to speak two or three times.

In Saskatchewan our ferries belong to the Provincial Government, and this section would give rise to disputes as to who is to arrange the contract, whether the mail carrier or the Federal Government. Who is to arrange the contract?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The contract may be made between the man who owns or operates the ferry and the Postmaster General.
Is there any penalty attached to a refusal to make a contract?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There is a general penal clause in the Post Office Act in regard to refusal by any one to carry His Majesty's mails. That clause would be operative.

In that case quite a hardship will arise, especially in the province from which I come. We have a number of large rivers that are crossed by ferries; there are few bridges. When the ice is running out in the spring or forming in the fall it is almost impossible to operate those ferries. In such a case would the ferryman be liable to a penalty for not operating?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No natural obstruction, or obstruction by act of God, would render any ferryman liable.

The section provides: "Every ferryman shall upon request and without delay, convey over his ferry," etc. No provision is made for delay on occasions when it would be difficult to operate the ferry. For instance, it might not be possible to operate at night. Then, when the logs are being driven the crossing of the stream by the ferry is often a very hazardous operation. Many of the small rivers in our part of the country are crossed by a ferry which is attached to wire cables stretched from one side of the river to the other, the boat drifting across with the current. When the logs are running down there might easily be times when the operation of the ferry would be very dangerous. I would like to know how the minister intends to work that out.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The contract, I suppose, would provide that the mail couriers should be ferried across only at reasonable times and at reasonable hours. Certainly the inability of a ferryman to cross owing to obstructions or difficulties by reason of weather conditions would not render him liable to penalty. The mail courier would have to accept the usual terms and conditions applying to the ferry service. There would be no liability on the part of the ferryman in the case my hon. friend mentions.

The language of this section would appear to be a little vague. It reads:
Every ferryman shall, upon request and without delay, convey over his ferry any courier or other person travelling with the mail, and the carriage and horse or horses or other vehicle employed in carrying the same; and the sum to be paid for such service may be fixed by contract.
If the ferryman refuses to carry the mail under the ordinary conditions, who shall determine the price? It cannot be the department; it cannot be the ferryman. What would be the procedure?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I am informed that practically every ferryman has a tariff of fees which he charges to the general public. Well, that would be the binding tariff.
In municipalities in our provinces the operation of no ferry is authorized unless there is a schedule of rates for the public. I do not know how it is in the other provinces.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I am informed that that is general throughout Canada.

Who, then, shall determine the price if the ferryman for some



reason, say on account of inconvenient hours, refuses to carry the mail across the river? Is there provision for an arbitration? Is there any reference to the courts?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not see how any difficulty can arise. No ferryman could be asked to make anything but his ordinary trips; all we are entitled to is regular trade at his regular rates. If a man should bluntly say he would not do it, there is a clause in the Act which will penalize him.

There might be circumstances under which the man could not do it. For instance, I know of ferries which are not equipped to carry horses, whereas this Bill provides that the ferryman shall convey the courier and his horse and wagon. I have no objection to the general clause, but how does the minister expect to settle disputes? Will he send an inspector or an officer of the department to find out what the usual charge is and then have the courier tender that to the ferryman?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is the idea. The post office inspector will find out what his tariff of fees is for ordinary trade and we shall pay him the same as he charges to the public.
Has there been any hold-up necessitating this legislation?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No, but there has been an arbitration, I am told-most unsatisfactory and long drawn out-and we may be threatened with others. Of course, a man could not be asked to build a special equipment or operate special boats to carry the Government business; if he has not the equipment he could not be expected to convey the mails unless a new contract were made for that purpose.

Will
this measure apply to the Government ferry on the Strait of Canso where the Minister of Railways is the ferryman?
My hon. friend does not need to be reminded that there are many ferries in Nova Scotia subsidized by the present Murray Government where there is no water.
I was not aware of that.

Is it the intent of this clause to prevent the payment of subsidies in future in respect of mail service?
	.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No, I do not think it has any bearing on that point.

Owing to my poor knowledge of the English language I had to employ the aid of Webster to find out the meaning of the word "ferry." It means:
A place of crossing; a place of passage where persons or things are carried across a river, arm of the sea, etc., in a boat; a vessel in which passengers and goods are conveyed over narrow waters; a ferry-boat.
When I mentioned a moment ago the river St. Lawrence, Quebec city and the island of Orleans I contended that the service operated between Quebec city and that island was not a ferry service. My complaint is that the Post Office Department has treated that service as if it were an ordinary ferry service and has never paid a cent for the transportation of the mails between those points. In years past it was otherwise, and quite properly so, but during the last two years or so it has been treated quite differently. I would like the' minister to look into this matter with a view to doing justice to a company which is carrying large quantities of mail without any remuneration whatever.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I will take pleasure in directing the attention of the Postmaster General to the point raised by my hon. friend. It is a matter of legal interpretation whether it is a ferry or not a ferry. I would give my off-hand opinion that it is a ferry, notwithstanding the fact that there is a distance of seven miles to travel. However, I may be wrong. If it is not a ferry, as my hon. friend contends, this section has no application to it.
Who is the Postmaster General?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.
May I be permitted, Mr. Chairman, to put a question bearing on clause 1?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it the unanimous
consent of the committee that the hon. member for Maisonneuve may refer to clause 1?

I approve clause 1,
because I found that, in years gone by, this post insurance business was done exclusively by American companies. Now I see that there is on the Order Paper notice by the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) of a resolution dealing with insurance companies. I want to know, in connection with this, if those American insurance companies who were dealing in post insurance

will continue the business in view of the fact that the Post Office Department is now taking this business to itself.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
There is in the Act, so
far as I know, no prohibition to prevent any insurance company, if it so desires, from doing post insurance business in this country. The question whether it is necessary to put any restrictions on this business is a matter for discussion and consideration.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I think, up to the limitation mentioned in the clause, my hon. friend is correct. If I had my way, I would give a monopoly to the Post Office Department of insurance of mailable packages up to $100; but as regards the tremendous number of packages which go through the mails with very large amounts of money in them, private corporations should still be entitled to insure those. Look at the shipments of bonds and cash far in excess of $100. Up to $100, I think, it would be practicable to grant a monopoly to the Post Office Department for insurance. That is only my opinion; I have never heard the matter discussed, but my hon. friend's suggestion seems very reasonable.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When shall the Bill be read the third time?	[DOT]

Next sitting of the
House. In the meanwhile I would ask my hon. friend to look into this question and see if it should not be enacted that post office insurance should belong to the Post Office Department exclusively up to $100, the receipts appertaining naturally to the Post Office Department.
135i

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It might be more appropriate to put that in the Insurance Act.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is quite competent
for the minister to move the third reading now, if he so desires.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Next sitting of the
House.
