stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Right Hon. Sir George Foster (Minister of Trade and Commerce) for the second reading of Bill No. 61, respecting a certain trade agreement between His Majesty and the President of the French Republic.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think the
hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) is particularly interested in this Bill, and if he had known it was coming up to-night, I am sure he would have been here.

Does my hon.
friend think it wise to let him know that it is coming up to-night?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I will let him know at once.
We will go on and discuss it; we shall not get very far before he comes up.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On clause 1-short title.

It might be
well for me to make a short statement with reference to the general purport of the agreement itself, before we go into the different clauses of the Bill.
A little louder please.

Yes, my voice will rise as I go on. The committee knows quite well that in 1907 and 1909, not to speak of the preceding treaty, or trade, arrangement between Canada and France, there were under negotiation the conventions so-called of 1907 and 1909. They went into effect in the year 1910, and they have been in effect from that time until their cancellation which took place in 1920. After the war had gone on for a little time, France gave notice to all countries with which she had treaty agreements, that she would hold herself free to undertake new negotiations resulting from changes which took place on account of and during the war, and in order to make herself free for that kind of negotiation, notice was

given of the cancellation of those treaties. She accompanied that declaration as regards Canada, and, I think, as regards many other countries, with the statement that it was not because France was indisposed to retain treaty arrangements with reference to trade, but that she wanted to hold herself free as I have stated, the arrangement to go on in the meantime, subject to cancellation by either side on three months' notice. Therefore, the convention was kept in force for a year and a half or more after the notice of which I spoke had been made, on the condition that either party might abrogate or annul the arrangement by giving three months' notice.
In the course of the tariff arrangements which were necessary in Canada in order to get as large a revenue as possible from some articles, particularly those articles with reference to which there was a special schedule in the French convention allowing a certain list of articles to come in at a lower rate than even the intermediate rata, it was found, as that was a minimum tariff below all other tariffs in respect to those goods, that all nations with mostfavoured-nation treaties had a right to the same minimum as France. Therefore, not only did that class of goods which came in from France at a low rate diminish our possible revenues but like goods coming in especially from Switzerland and Japan such as silks, embroideries and all that kind of goods on which they enjoyed as well the minimum made a larger hole in the revenue than it was thought should be allowed during the period of the war. Therefore we came to the conclusion, as I stated, to take advantage of the three months' notice; we gave the three months' notice to France, and in June of 1920, or thereabouts, the treaty so far as Canada was concerned was denounced, and from that time until this importations from France have been carrying the maximum rate of duty in all cases. France, however, was not anxious that there should be a complete severance of trade interchanges betwen the two countries. Canada also desired, if possible, that they could be carried on in some modified form. Under the circumstances it was absolutely impossible, and is at the present moment, to undertake to make a general treaty arrangement with France, or in fact with any other European country, owing to the disorganized state of trade and the emergencies in every one of these countries causing duties to be changed frequently, and in some cases greatly increased, revenues being very much needed.

After certain pourparlers, undertaken and carried on for a number of months, we came at last to a conclusion, when I was in Paris on my way back from Geneva, and agreed upon a modus vivendi or trade agreement by which, subject to four months' notice, certain interchanges of articles should take place between the two countries along a certain line of duties.
The committee will remember that we had three schedules in the convention of 1907 and 1909. One was schedule "A." Under that schedule France imposed only the minimum tariff upon the products of Canada named therein; there were some 152 different items. These had been chosen because they were the items for which Canada would be most likely to find a market in the French Republic. Schedule "A," then marked the goods of Canadian origin which could be taken into France under the minimum tariff. Then came schedule "B"; that contained a list of selected articles, the origin of which was in France, which could be imported into Canada under our intermediate tariff. Then there was a special schedule "C," containing a list of articles, not very large in number, but fairly important in the matter of export for France, on which there were special duties lower than the intermediate tariff.
Now let us see what has taken place with reference to these three schedules. As I stated, on schedule "A" French maximum tariff went into force against importations from Canada and France was in a position to place all these articles under her maximum tariff. With reference to schedules "B" and "C," imports from France into this country, they also came under our maximum tariff on the denunciation of the convention of 1907. The arrangement which was ultimately arrived at was that of the 152 articles in schedule "A," which after the denunciation of the treaty became subject to the French maximum tariff, but which under the old convention went in under the minimum tariff, all except twelve should again be allowed in under the French minimum tariff. Under the present arrangement, these 12 articles are allowed into France at less than the maximum duty, the respective duties at which they are allowed into that country being shown opposite each item in schedule 1 of the Bill before the committee.
With reference to the articles in schedule "C," which had the lowest rating when imported into Canada, these now come in under our intermediate tariff. We give to

those French products the intermediate tariff and France, in return for that, gives us the minimum tariff on all the 152 articles in schedule "A" in the former Convention except twelve. France gives us, in addition to that, a lower tariff, either the minimum, or one lower than the maximum, on the articles in schedule 2 of this Bill. To the most of them she gives the minimum tariff, and to a number of them a tariff which is less than the maximum by a percentage of the difference between the minimum and the maximum duty. That is marked opposite each article.
That about covers the main features of the arrangement we have made. This modus vivendi is with France alone. The convention of 1907 and of 1909 took in the dependencies of France, and gave to articles imported from the French dependencies the same schedule we gave to France, and vice versa, our goods entering these French possessions enjoyed their minimum tariff. The arrangement now is made simply and solely between France and Canada as respects either exports or imports. Its purpose is to carry on as extensive trade exchanges as we can, and to fcontinue the favourable relations we have had, without going back to the maximums in both tariffs; with the condition attached, that by four months' notice either country is in a position to abrogate the arrangement.

I call my hon. friend's attention again to the form of this document. When it was brought down at an earlier stage we discovered that it was in, shall I say, a very slovenly condition, and I am sorry to say that it is yet imperfect. I think it will be admitted that if we are dealing with an important matter of this sort we are entitled to exact copies of the documents in question. My hon. friend must be mistaken when he says that this schedule to the Bill is an exact copy of the treaty. I cannot imagine that it is, for I never knew a treaty to be in this form. My hon. friend will tell me, no doubt, that what is left out is of no great importance; but that does not meet the situation. Will he say again that the schedule on page 2 of the Bill is an exact copy of the agreement which he is asking us to ratify?

The schedule to the Bill as it appears here is an exact copy, from beginning to end, of the arrangement as it was agreed to and signed. My hon. friend refers to a paper which
was placed before the House some time ago. That was not the Bill, nor did it pretend to be a copy of it. It was printed and distributed to the members mainly, I suppose, to give information. The Bill was introduced after the resolution was passed, and as it now appears it is an exact copy of the arrangement as made and signed in Paris.

My hon. friend says that the previous document was not a Bill.
I have it in my hand; it is headed: "An Act Respecting a Certain Trade Agreement between His Majesty and the President of the French Republic." That was the document that was circulated in the House, and it is in the form of a Bill. However, I am not pressing the point in regard to the form in which that document appeared, but I again say that if the agreement attached to this Bill No. 61 is an exact copy of the document which my hon. friend calls an arrangement, but which is virtually a treaty, I am amazed at its form. I never knew a treaty to be in the form of this one, and I am persuaded that my hon. friend is under a misapprehension and has really not given us an exact copy of the document.

I cannot do
more than give my hon. friend my word.
I do not doubt the hon. [DOT]gentleman's word at all.
If the hon. member has any misgivings, I will show him the original.
I should like to see it.

I do not
imagine that he questions my word.
I do not require more than the hon. member's word, but it would be interesting to see the original.
Will the minister look at the schedule as printed? Does he not think that there is a clerical error in the first article?

The copy which my hon. friend has handed me is a French version. Now, these documents are generally done in English and French. I am glad that my right hon. friend has such an ample knowledge of the French language that he can manage without an English copy; but in deference to some of us who are not as proficient as he in the French tongue, he might give us an English copy. This is a case, perhaps, in

which we do not want too much French domination.

The English
copy is an exact and definite translation of the original copy in French, which the hon. member has in his hands. The French
copy he has contains everything together with the names of the signatories.
Why should not a document of this character be printed in both French and English, and copies of both versions submitted to hon. members? Will my hon. friend tell me that?

Yes, if you
stick at that.

Well, the point is
worth discussing.

The agreement was made between myself and the French authorities, and the text, which was in French, is signed by both parties. I left for London, taking with me one copy of the French version, and when in London I received the assent of the Government to sign the treaty. I signed it in London and sent the French copy back, through the Foreign Office, to Paris. The English translation as we have it here will be signed by the French authorities and two copies will then be forwarded to me, one to be signed by me and sent back, the other to remain in my possession. So that we shall then have both English and French copies, signed. '

I do not want to press what may seem to some to be an unimportant point, but does my hon. friend suggest that he is doing right when * he brings down what purports to be a correct copy of a treaty, and gives us only the French version? We are not all as proficient as my hon. friend in the French language, and those of us who unfortunately, are in that unhappy position, ought to have an English copy. After all, the English speaking members have some rights in this House. What is the reason we have no English copy?

My hon. friend has the English translation, as well as the original, in the French language, and the names of the four signatories." He has everything, so that if he had the original signatories on the English copy he would get no more information than he has now, nor can I get any further light on

the subject by reason of the little knowledge of French that I have.

If one wanted to be technical, one might ask the minister what the meaning of the following is:
Signed:	Hardinge of Penshurst, H.M.S.
"Ambassador."
What does that mean?
I did not notice the fact before, but my hon. friend evidently has the signatories on that copy too.

Yes; I happen to have two copies but the signatories do not correspond exactly. I am not suggesting that there is any material difference, but I am asking that the business of the House be done in a business-like way and that we be given exact copies of documents. I do think that we ought to have an exact copy. I have one copy with the signatures. Another printed copy, which also purports to be a correct translation, is signed "Hardinge of Penshurst, H.M.S. Ambassador." That is on one of the printed copies and not on the other. I confess I am not sure what the "H.M.S. Ambassador" means.
Were there two printed copies?
I can assure my hon. friend I got two printed copies-one that I have received now and one that my hon. friend circulated before.

My hon. friend is sticking at a mighty little point. I gave no orders at all for the printing of the document that my hon. friend got into his hands the other day and about which he has raised a deuce of a row. That was printed by somebody, but was not the Bill which I presented, because the Bill had not been introduced at that time. The Bill as introduced was printed and my hon. friend now has a copy "of it in his hand. I find that he has a copy with the signatures, as printed, as well.
Surely.

Then my hon. friend might drop the thing he got before which was not authorized and which was not a copy of my Bill. He has now an exact copy of the Bill and he can lay the other sheet aside. I am sorry it got into his hands if it riles him so.
It has not riled me.

It seems to have worked that way somehow or other. He has

now exactly in English what appears in the French version. What is the signature that he has on the treaty in French? The one I have is signed " Hardinge of Pen-shurst " and " G. E. Foster."
This is signed "Hardinge of Penshurst, H.M.S. Ambassador;" and " G. E. Foster."
My hon. friend had better drop the other little sheet. It is not an authorized copy, I am fully satisfied.

My hon. friend seems to think it is making a great disturbance to ask that documents-solemn documents, that we require to deal with in the House- shall be presented to us in correct form. To do that is not raising a hulabaloo; it is nothing but fair to the House that the documents we are called upon to deal with should be absolutely in correct form. My hon. friend has said that he did not authorize these documents. He did not say that the other day: he told us the Bill had been printed. Pie told us that the treaty had been printed and I find it has been sent out in a different form. In one case, as I have already stated, it is signed "Hardinge of Penshurst, H.M.S. Ambassador." I presume that is correct, but I am only calling for legitimate information when I ask what is the meaning of these initials.
I suppose they would represent His Britannic Majesty's Ambassador.

I do not think they stand for " His Britannic Majesty's Ambassador. " Perhaps the initials in my hon. friend's copy are different from those in mine. There is another material difference. I am curious to know how important business of this character could be presented in such-i wish to say it without being offensive -a very slovenly manner. When we call the attention of my hon. friend to the difference between these documents he replies that they could not have got here through his action. He told us at first that he had brought down the treaty, and when we drew his attention to the fact that the document in our possession was not what it purported to be my hon. friend repudiated it.

Will my hon. friend allow me to make another explanation? I had no more idea what he had in his hand than I have of the sort of trumpet the Archangel Gabriel will sound when he comes on the Last Day. I know I had
ordered the preparation of the Bill, and I had a copy of the Bill in my hand when the resolution was introduced. My supposition was that the hon. gentleman had exactly the same printed document that 1 had but it appears that he had not. Again I say to him that I authorized no distribution of documents such as he speaks of. What was taken and printed was the document that I sent to be embodied in the Bill itself, and it seems to have happened that it was printed in order to give information as soon as possible to the members of the House.

My hon. friend supposes I have some document that was unauthorized. I had only the same document that every other hon. member of the House got; it was laid on the Table and my hon. friend at the time it was done said he had brought down the document. The difference in this matter may not be important in itself, but I do say that in a matter of this kind business ought to be done in a more regular and complete form.

I never said I laid the document on the Table. What I stated was that documents were laid on the Table. There was laid on the Table an exact copy of the treaty. That was done when I was not here and that is what I suppose the hon. member had in his hand.
When I asked for this treaty I was certainly informed that it had been laid on the Table.
It was laid on the Table by the Prime Minister.

The document laid on the Table was the document I have in my hand, the document that every other member got. My hon. friend endeavours to convey the impression that I had some sort of a strange document that other hon. gentlemen did not have. It is somewhat inconceivable that this document would have emanated from any other department than that of the hon. gentleman himself. Having called attention to that, suppose we now try to find out what "H.M.S. Ambassador," as printed on one document, means. If I understood my hon. friend's explanation correctly, it was that all the concessions that were granted to France under the former treaty are continued, is that correct?
I did not catch my hon. friend's question.

I understood from my hon. friend's explanation that all the con-

cessions contained in our former treaty with Prance are continued to that country-[DOT]
Oh, no.

Except as to the
colonies.

I said quite the opposite. I might repeat, as my hon. friend was not here when I gave the explanation that as regards schedule "A" "Exports from Canada to France " in convention of 1907 the minimum tariff applies to all these articles with the exception of twelve. With reference to the articles in schedules "B" and "C" "Imports from France to Canada" the intermediate tariff is given. That is instead of getting less than the intermediate tariff on any they get the intermediate tariff, and that only, on all.
That is on goods coming into Canada?
Into Canada.

I am sorry I was not present to hear the first part of my hon. friend's explanation. Under schedule one, do I understand that Canadian products are not to benefit any more by the minimum tariff, that is Canadian products going into France?

The minimum
applies on all articles save twelve.

When the percentage
is given, does that mean the percentage of the total duty? For example, here is a list of articles which we are told are to come in under fifteen per cent. The column is headed "Percentages" and below appears the figures "15 per cent" what does that mean-fifteen per cent of what?

That means
fifteen per cent, as stated in the agreement, of the difference between the maximum and the minimum duties. There is a maximum duty and there is a minimum duty. The difference between the two is taken and fifteen per cent of that constitutes the rebate for that article. My hon. friend will see that that percentage never varies. The maximum may vary, the minimum may vary and consequently the result of the percentage may vary, but it is always the same percentage-

Would the minister
take a specific case and work it out. I am something like the Oxford undergraduate who said he did not have the low cunning to understand figures; therefore I would like to see a specific case worked out.
My hon. friend is not ignorant in that respect. The way it is arrived at is this. Supposing that the maximum is eighty francs, remember, in kilograms, taking the units-
Give us the maximum and the minimum.

Yes. Supposing the maximum tariff is eighty francs and supposing the minimum tariff is twenty francs; subtract twenty from eighty and that leaves you sixty, and you will get fifteen per cent of that as a rebate.
Of the sixty?
Yes.

Would my hon. friend give us the effect of this as applied to some articles of Canadian export in order that we may be able to see at a glance what the concession amounts to? I would not ask my hon. friend to give us that information at the moment, but before the matter is disposed of I think he might have a statement prepared of the duties imposed on a number of representative articles that we are able to export to France so that we may see the measure of the difference we are getting under this concession.

I can give my hon. friend the difference in so far as regards products in schedule 1, which, with the exception of some three or four in schedule 2, are the only products to which the percentage principle applies. The others are all on a minimum tariff.

I really think, having regard to the class of information which my right hon. friend used to ask when he was not on the side that he is on now, that he ought to give us further information in printed form in order that we may study this important document and see its effects. I hope my right hon. friend will have such a document prepared.
I will be very glad to do that.
Coming to schedule 2, what would be the meaning of the initials "T.M.T." about the middle of the schedule? They occur in two places.

If my hon. friend will strike out the first "T" he will get "M.T."-minimum tariff. That is again an example of the fallibility of the human instrument. The "T" got in through the printer's press somehow or other-the de-

vil was in it I suppose. Of course it should be "M.T."

I know if that was the case in any document brought down in former days no one in the House was more keen to observe it and show the enormity of the blunder than my hon. friend. So, he must not object if we insist upon this treaty being correct to a "t."

My hon.
friend is quite aware that when a bill comes before the House and is gone through section" by section, it is up to the man who is putting it through to see that little errors are corrected. Now, this little one will be corrected when we come to it.

I want to say to my right hon. friend that it is up to the minister in charge of a bill, and especially an important bill to ratify a treaty, to see that he gives the House correct information at the beginning and not force us to draw it out of him in this way. I; hope he will take a wider interpretation as to the duty of the minister in the case, and not merely ask the Clerk of the House to discover whether the minister is doing his work well. I do not think it is fair to impose that responsibility on the Clerk.
But suppose the Bill had been so very, very perfect, my hon. friend would have had no ground of criticism, and that would be awful.
I know. I do not want to criticise the minister. I think he will find many occasions when I have had to compliment him. On the whole I have been rather a friendly critic.

I think you
have been splendid on the whole.
It is "M.T."- minimum tariff.
We get the full minimum in that case?
Yes.
I suppose this is virtually a new treaty? The old treaty had expired.

The old treaty had expired. Yet I think this is absolutely true, that the French Government has treated Canadian importations up to the present time under the old convention, if not in all cases, in most cases, not because she was obliged to, but because she was willing to.

While we are all
aware of the efficacy of a soft answer in turning away wrath, yet we Would like the answer not to be so soft as to prevent us hearing the words of wisdom that fall from the lips of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Hear, hear.

Before that question of initials is finally settled, I wish to contribute to an accurate interpretation of those letters "H.M.S." I listened to the exchanges between my two hon. friends with very great attention. My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's suggested that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce said those letters might mean ''His Britannic Majesty."

I quoted that from
my hon. friend.

That is just what I say. But I am positive that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce never used the word "Britannic" I want to clear him of that aspersion. He could not have used the word "Britannic" as representing "H," "M" or ''S." He is too good a scholar to do that. So the only mystery is about the "S." Now I cannot accept the explanation of my hon. friend from Brome, because we all know that "Hardinge" is not a ship, and it has just occurred to me that "H.M.S." may mean "His Majesty's Signatory." If I havn not found the right interpretation, I have found something that would be quite right-
You have got your letters right.

Yes. "S"
stands for signatory, and "Hardinge" is a signatory. If that will help the researches in this matter I think it is my duty to put my thought at the disposal of the minister; and I do hope if he cannot find out the real meaning of "S" he will take my suggestion and simply call "H.M.S." His Majesty's Signatory.

If I ignore the first document and confine myself to the second

one, it purports by the title to be "an Act respecting a certain trade agreement between His Majesty and the President of the French Republic." I must not he too positive, because one sometimes in the hurry does not see things, but so far as I can observe there is not a word within the four corners of this treaty which has any mention of His Majesty in any shape or form, and if you strike out this "H.M.S." which my hon. friend suggested might stand for His Majesty^ Ship or something of that sort, there is absolutely no reference to His Majesty the King in the whole transaction from beginning to end. Am I correct?

The reading
there is very plain, as my hon. friend says.
My hon. friend does not deny it?
I cannot.
Perhaps it is an evidence of our new nationhood that we now make treaties without reference to His Majesty?
Yes.

Then I suggest my
hon. friend should change the title of this Bill. It is not an agreement between His Majesty and the President of the French Republic; there is no reference to His Majesty in it. Surely it is making improper use of His Majesty's name. If His Majesty is not worth mentioning in the document itself I do not think we ought to make His Majesty responsible by putting his name in the title. In that respect it is a rather remarkable document. However, I simply call my right hon. friend's attention to it; I hope that before the matter goes through he will be able to give us some further information with regard to the point I have suggested.

If my hon.
friend has sufficiently digested the original, may I ask that he send it over to me?

My hon. friend has not given us an English copy. I must say I do not think that is quite satisfactory. I do not suggest that there is any difference, but it is a strange proceeding, it seems to me, to have a document of this kind brought down to us in French and not in English. Generally it is the other way; our French friends have reason to complain at times that documents are brought down in English and not in French. I want to stand 
now for the rights of the English in this matter; I do not think we are getting a fair show.

I am very
glad to have made it possible for my hon. friend to feel the lash, as well as other English representatives on that side.

Any concession which
is granted to the French Republic under this treaty will be given to many other nations, will it not?
It will be given to all most favoured nations.
Do those other nations give us compensation for anything they may get by virtue of this treaty?

Those other
nations all have most favoured nation treaties with us and under them, as my hon. friend knows, they get the treatment accorded to any new nation that comes in under the treaty.

Can my right hon.
friend give a list of those nations?

Argentina,
Colombia, Denmark, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Venezuela and Japan. Three other countries were given special advantages when my hon. friend was Minister of Finance; I think it would he about the time that the French convention was ratified- that is, Belgium, the Netherlands and Italy. Belgium and the Netherlands were given the intermediate tariff, on the same list of goods, if I remember rightly, as was allowed to come in by France and Italy on a less extended list. They still get the same advantages.
All these eight nations my right hon. friend first named get concessions under this treaty and give nothing in return?

France gets
no concession under this treaty that is not already given to these countries; consequently they do not benefit by the present arrangement made with France. If afterwards we give to any other nation treaty or tariff benefits lower than these, the most favoured nations come in and enjoy the same.

I note that quite a
change has come over tny hon. friend with respect to these favoured nations. When the reciprocity treaty-not as we discussed yesterday, but as it was years ago -was presented to this House, the late

Prime Minister, then leader of the Opposition, and hon. gentlemen generally who were then in Opposition made a great fuss oyer the fact that the concessions which were granted to the United States would have to be granted also to a large number of other nations. But we have here a recognition of the favoured nation treaty. The right hon. gentleman's statement is quite correct; any concession that has come to France in this matter will be given to all the favoured nations. My right hon. friend, therefore, has come to an appreciation of the value of these favoured nation treaties which he did not entertain at that time. It was considered by our friends at that time to be a very serious offence on our part when we agreed to make any concessions to these nations without their giving us something in return. I do not see anything wrong in it; I simply remind my right hon. friend that his point of view is quite changed. [DOT]

My hon. friend will never fail to remind me; I observe that he is going to perform that duty to the letter. I shall not go into the discussions of 1910 and 1911 on the reciprocity treaty. Circumstances differ from time to time. We have to-day ten nations that have most favoured nation treatment. If to-morrow the question came to be discussed whether we should give to another nation lower rates of duty on a list of articles than we are now giving to most favoured nations, I would argue, as I do now, that we would have to give similar reductions to those ten nations and that we would have to be mighty careful before we made the reduction to the eleventh nation. That, if my memory serves me correctly, is what I was arguing in 1911.

Although the treaty
does not seem to be over-generous, I am satisfied with it so far as it goes. I appreciate the difficulties met by the right hon. gentleman when he went to France to revise the old treaty. All those who have been in Europe of late know that the French Government is facing very serious difficulties on account of the reparations problem, the devastated areas, the depreciation of French currency, and other serious considerations resulting from the war. The French Government, therefore, are somewhat diffident about entering into definite commercial arrangements with other countries. Without going into the details of the treaty-we shall have an opportunity to do so at a later stage-I may say that
I am gratified to know that the Canadian Government has revived our trade agreement with France, though it is modified in some ways. Indeed, if I had my own way, having regard to the sacrifices made by France during the war, I would he disposed to give France, if not the British preference, the next to it. Of all the allies, France is the most deserving. Besides, during the unfortunate period of the war the French people traded extensively with Canada. We have only to look at the figures which are to be found in the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Whilst, in 1914, imports from France amounted to $14,276,000; in 1918, they fell to $5,274,000; in 1919, they were $3,632,000 and, in 1920, there is a revival; I see that in that year we imported from France goods to the value of $10,609,122. This is just a fair business on our part with France; but look at what we are selling to France, what an important market it is for Canadian manufacturers and exporters generally. Whilst, in 1914, Canada exported to France goods to the value of $3,632,444; during the war, in 1918, of necessity of course because of the war, Canada exported to France goods to the value of $210,526,297. In 1919, a year after the armistice, I see that, not-wnthstanding the cessation of hostilities, Canada exported to France goods to the value of $96,103,142, and in 1920, without a treaty, without any special favour, France opened her ports to Canadian produce to the extent of $61,106,938. This is in spite of all a most gratifying result. After the United States and Great Britain, France is the best customer we have in the world and surely that market is worth cultivating.
I am sure, if the right hon. gentleman will take under his especial care the administration of this treaty, there is a strong probability that we may not only maintain, but increase this very interesting figure of $61,000,000, which represents our total exports to France during the last fiscal year.
But my right hon. friend, if he will administer this treaty as he should, will do what he was advised to do the other evening. I have been in France on several occasions and I must say that it is not possible to expect that trade with Canada will undergo any great expansion, excluding, of course, the period of the war, if only one solitary agent is maintained in France. As things stand at present, we have just one little office, in the Commissioner General's office, in Paris, with one agent. France has a population of thirty-nine or forty million. Paris, of course, is a great centre;

one might say that, on Continental Europe, Paris is the great centre, but Paris is not all Prance. There are in the north and in the south, in the east and in the west, very important commercial centres in France. The most important centre of commerce in France from all times has been the northern section. Take cities like Lille, Le Havre;" take cities like Bordeaux, Marseilles, two of the largest ports of the world, and Lyons. If you have no representatives in those cities, which are the nerve centres of French commerce and industry, you cannot develop those channels of trade which you are seeking to establish between Canada and France. I know, of course, that you cannot depend only on your trade agents; but trade agents, well trained, having exhibits of Canadian products, trade agents who are absolute masters of the French language, will in France be of very great help to our manufacturers and traders generally in Canada. The present trade organization from the point of view of the Department of Trade and Commerce is next to nil. Mr. Barre, our representative in Paris, whom I have seen at work, is a most excellent gentleman. He saw some service during the late war, and he is doing his very best; but he cannot be ubiquitous, and he cannot answer to all calls that are made upon him by French business men. Therefore, I would urge upon my right hon. friend to do something in the way of promoting Canadian trade in that great country.
As my right hon. friend stated the other day, there is, in that train exhibit which will soon roll on the Canadian and the French railway systems, a hope that there will be an interest revived in both countries as regards trade possibilities. But something else must be done. I must say that the right hon. gentleman had Canada fairly well represented at the great Lyons fair, and from the reports which I have read, published by boards of trade, the Canadian exhibits created a splendid effect at that fair. But that is not sufficient; that can strike only one particular spot. There should be a more "live wire" organization all throughout France. Let us not forget that France is the third country on the list of our customers; it comes next to the United States and Great Britain, and trade with that country should be encouraged as much as possible. It has displaced Germany. On the whole I see with pleasure that this treaty has been negotiated. It has not the same flavour as the old treaty. I think the old treaty was more favourable 
but, of course, I understand the difficulties with which my right hon. friend had to contend when he went to France at the beginning of last winter.
There is another point, which I do not wish to dilate on this evening because we may have another opportunity to discuss the whys and wherefores of it, and that is as to the final signatories of the treaty. For my part, I am a strong Canadian, and I do not object to His Majesty the King being a signatory to that treaty, through the British Ambassador in Paris, or eve1! through the instrumentality of the Foreign Office in London, but what I object to is the subterfuge of my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) who of late has been stating ad nauseam that Canada was a nation, that there was such a thing as a Canadian national, and that we enjoyed almost sovereign powers. Yet in the case of this treaty, which is the renewal of an old treaty, we find that my right hon. friend, fresh from the Geneva Conference, where the sovereign rights of Canada were supposed to have been proclaimed throughout the world, knowing the value of words and not carried away by the Celtic imagination of his colleague the right hon. the Minister of Justice, goes direct to the Foreign Office in London and from there by a circuitous route to the British Ambassador in Paris to get the agreement signed. It is through the British representative in the Old Country and in France that this treaty has found life. Once more I say, I do not object at all to the British Ambassador or the Foreign Office in London intervening in a purely commercial agreement, but I do object to all this subterfuge of the right hon. Minister of Justice as to Canada being a nation. We may be a nation in his imagination, but when we get down to hard-pan we find that we are still a Dominion, with no sovereignty, and that this treaty would be non-existent but for the signatures on the parchment of Hardinge of Penshurst before that of George E. Foster.
Mr. Chairman, on the whole, I shall support the treaty. I hope, however, that as the matter is a very important one, my right hon. friend will do us the favour of giving my hon. friend to my left his rights, in this case, an English version of the treaty. I stand for the rights of the English majority, as I am sure my right hon. friend would stand for the rights of the French minority, and I therefore appeal to him to give my hon. friend the English version of the French Treaty.

If my hon. friend would consent, I should also like to have copies of the correspondence which is annexed to the original treaty printed and distributed to the members of the House, as I am sure it would be very interesting.

I have not had very much time to study the treaty, but I have looked over it. My constituency and the part of the Dominion from which I come is especially interested in the fish trade, and I was curious to know if my right hon. friend had endeavoured to get the minimum tariff or get put on the free list any articles that we sell largely to France. I am not familiar with the French tariff, but my right hon. friend is no doubt aware of what articles are on the free list. In glancing over the articles mentioned in schedule 2, which are to enjoy the benefit of a minimum tariff, I was struck by the fact that these are not the articles that Canada is selling to France.
I have the report here of the Department of Trade and Commerce showing the trade we did with France in 1920. I have studied that report to find out what gpods we have been selling to France. My hon. friend the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) has stated that last year we sold $21,000,000 of our products to France, and those products according to this Blue Book published by my right hon. friend, are cattle, horses, sheep, apples, automobiles, breadstuffs including barley, oats, oatmeal, pease, wheat, wheat flour; calcium carbide, coal, fish, canned lobsters, canned salmon, hay, leather, aluminium, copper, iron ore, lead, nickel, milk, paper, provisions, meats, seeds, textiles, vegetables and wood.
Now the articles in the schedule seem to be articles that we do not sell to France.
I cannot see very much benefit in a treaty of that kind. If my right hon. friend had been able to secure some concessions to Canada in respect of articles that we sell to France, the treaty might be of importance to the trade of this country. I would like my right hon. friend to explain how it is that not a single article in this schedule appears in the list of articles that our Canadian merchants and traders sold to France last year. The articles that are to enjoy the benefit of this minimum tariff under the agreement are feathers, for instance. Apparently we did not sell any feathers to France last year.

You will have
a chance. You can go into the feather business now.

I presume that the first item is a misprint and
that "nuts" was intended. There are a number of other articles such as prunes, petroleum, steam engines, boilers, heavy oils, padlocks, and so forth, but these do not appear to be articles that we sell to France. I would like to get some information from my right hon. friend as to the efforts that he made to secure some concessions for the natural products of Canada, such as fish, canned salmon and lobsters, oats, flour and wheat, if these_ articles are not already on the free list in Fi ance I should like some information on that phase of the treaty.

My hon. friend has just confined himself to schedule 2. That schedule embraces the articles on which, under the convention of 1907, Canada paid the maximum tariff and not the minimum or lower tariff. These articles have now been added to the list of articles, under the convention of 1907, upon which we formely got the minimum tariff. All the articles mentioned by my hon. friend will be found in the conventions of 1907 and 1909, and if he will read the Bill he will see that all of them, with the exception of 12, are still admitted to the minimum tariff. That is, 140 of the articles are admitted, as before, to the minimum tariff. What the hon. member has read in schedule 2 is over and above the concessions that we got before. These additions may or may not be valuable; some of them are very valuable; but, whether valuable or not, they are in addition to those we had under the convention of 1907. My hon. friend must read them both together in order to get the full list.

While correct in the main, the minister is inaccurate in one particular. It is true that fish, cattle and so forth, are all to be found in the old convention, and this treaty provides that these shall be continued, except as modified. Of course, in modifying that schedule, we are depriving ourselves of something which we had before. The articles memtioned by the member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), are still in the convention and are not in the least modified.
Those that are modified are in schedule 1.

With regard to cattle, I remember we had to make a supplementary treaty for that one particular thing. The French authorities were very much perturbed over our taking in fat cattle, and we had to make a supplementary treaty, which was a very trivial matter from our

point of 'view, although it was necessary. My hon. friend says that the articles in scheduled are articles which hitherto have not had the benefit of the minimum tariff and are additions which may or may not be of value. Among the things mentioned , that list is agricultural machinery, which is given as an addition to the articles on which we are to have the minimum. In that respect, the treaty is wrong. Agricultural machinery has the minimum tariff, and has had it since 1907. If my hon. friend will turn to the French convention, giving the list of Canadian products entitled to the French minimum tariff, he will find, in item 522, "agricultural machinery, motors not included''1. It is therefore erroneous to represent agricultural machinery as being something on which we shall now for the first time have the minimum tariff; it is not a new concession. In the old convention there is a long list of articles on which we got the benefit of the French minimum tariff. Under the new convention we do not get the same list, but only a portion of it; for the rest we get a modification. Well, in that case we are clearly losing something which we had under the other treaty. I am not opposing the treaty; I am merely endeavouring to have a clear understanding on this point, and I say that we are losing some things which we had previously. Now, what does France lose, apart from the fact that Algeria and the French colonies are not included? What is she going to give up in this deal? We have to give up something. Does France give up anything, or are we content that she should make no concession?

France does
give up something which is valuable. My hon. friend will recollect that Schedule "C" was a list of special articles upon which France received a special rate, below all our other rates. She gives that up entirely, and instead of getting that special rate she goes back to the intermediate rates on the articles specified in that schedule. The list of those articles is not very long, but it is very important to France. The articles embraced in the list are of importance to her export trade. The list comprises: Manufactures, of which silk is a component part, 321 per cent; ribbons of all kinds, 25 per cent; velvets of pure silk fabrics, 20 per cent; embroideries, lace, collars, collarets, all manufactures of lace, knittings, all cotton, silk, linen, 271 per cent. And then, with regard to No. 220, in medicinal and pharmaceutical and chemical preparations, books printed in the French language,

and champagne and other sparkling wines in bottles "A. B. C. and D.," she received a special tariff lower than our other tariffs. Then, under 163, she received a lower tariff on all wines of certain descriptions, A. B. and C. She received, under item 120, a special tariff on anchovy, sardines, sprats,
. and other fish packed in oil; and, under 86, she received a special rate on vegetables, tomatoes, etc. All these are articles which were of special importance to France, as my hon. friend knows.

My hon. friend is right when he says that the articles which France is supposed to give up are of importance to her trade. But where does he find any suggestion in the schedule that she is no longer to enjoy the special rates on these articles?

Article 1 of the Schedule reads:
Canada shall apply to products originating in and coming from France the most favourable tariffs and taxes that are or may be granted by ' Canada to the products of any third power, except those of the United Kingdom, or of British Dominions and possessions.
Now, the lowest minimum of our tariff to-day is the intermediate; we have nothing below that.

I see a difficulty here. The schedule does not specify the intermediate tariff; it does not fix any definite schedule of rates, and it will be difficult to determine precisely what it means. It does not clearly say that they are to give up anything.

We do not
specify the intermediate tariff, nor does France give us any definite schedule. The agreement simply says that she will give us the minimum.
No, not the minimum; she is to give the minimum, subject to modification.
She gives us the minimum on all articles except twelve, in schedule 1 of this particular modification. That leaves on the original list 140 of the articles that will get the minimum treatment.	-

It is quite clear under article 1 that we are to give the best treatment we can to foreign countries-that is essentially the most favoured nation principle. But it does not say the intermediate tariff, and I should almost think that there would be a little difficulty

in determining the effect of the clause for customs purposes. Was there any moment at which the old treaty had ceased to exist and there was no convention in existence, or was the treaty continued all the time?

It ceased by virtue of the denouncement made by Canada and it ceased in so far as imports from France into Canada were concerned at that date. France, I believe, continued for some time, on some articles at least, to allow Canadian exports to go in under the old convention rate-the minimum. I imagine that was because contracts had been made and these goods were being delivered under contract.

My hon. friend said a little while ago that favoured nation countries, a list of which he read, had these concessions for some time; but I would call his attention to the fact that favoured nation countries received that consideration through the French Treaty, and when the French Treaty ceased the favoured nations ceased to have any special rights. So he would not be correct in stating that all the favoured nations were entitled to have these concessions as in the past. It was a fact that we made a special treaty with France which obliged us to give to all the favoured nations the same rates; but when the treaty with France lapsed the favoured nation countries had no special claim upon us. That is why I ask my hon. friend as to whether there was a time when the treaty had actually expired.

They would
have no claim upon us for any reductions that were given to France by virtue of the convention of 1907. The fact that we gave to France, in schedule C, lower rates than any of the most favoured nations enjoyed on their exports brought them immediately to the enjoyment of the same privilege. When that treaty ceased they, of course, lost that privilege with regard to those articles.	*

When the French convention went out they lost any special claim upon Canada, and this country would be free to impose on them any tariff rates it pleased. There must have been a period which is now past, I presume, when we would have had the right to impose on all these nations different duties had we so desired.

May I ask who appointed the gentlemen who signed the treaty on behalf of Canada, and on behalf
of His Majesty? What authority did these gentlemen have to affix their signatures to the treaty?

The signatories, of course, on the French side were authorized by their government. I suppose they signed as ministers of the French Government. On our side I signed as representing Canada, and the British Ambassador signed as representing the Foreign Office and on behalf of His Majesty, which was necessary in order to make the treaty complete.

Well, this is not quite clear to me. The Bill says that this agreement was entered into at Paris by representatives appointed by His Majesty. Who acted for His Majesty in the appointment of the representatives? Was there an Order in Council appointing the two gentlemen who signed the treaty?

I was authorized, as far as I was concerned, by our own Government. That authority was intimated to the Foreign Office, through the Colonial Secretary, and the Foreign Office sent in a despatch to the British Ambassador in Paris to sign on behalf of His Majesty's Government.
Was there an Order in Council passed by the Imperial Government to that effect?
I saw none. In making that appointment I presume they followed the usual course.
It is stated here that the representatives were appointed by His Majesty. By what action of His Majesty were they appointed-only by a message from the Foreign Office?
Where is it stated that His Majesty appointed them?

In section 2. I think this is a very important matter. We are certainly entitled to all the particulars in that regard, especially in view of the announcement that we have made important steps on the road to nationhood. I want to know if there has been any change in the method of treaty making on the part of Canada with regard to this particular treaty?	[DOT]

There has
been no change.
Certainly not.

There has
been no change. The arrangement that was made at Washington, and the treaty that was made in 1907 by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) were negotiated with the privity of His Majesty's Government and were signed by the -ambassador representing Great Britain at Washington and also by the British Ambassador at Paris. The same thing was done here. There was no very great formality about it as far as I saw, or as far as I was concerned, but it was by the direction of the Foreign Office that the treaty was signed.

But my right hon.
friend knows that on the dates he has just mentioned we were considered to be a dependency by the United Kingdom. Now we are a sister nation. We have been told that we should be proud that we are a sister nation, enjoying absolute equality of status. Is it an evidence of that if we have to go to the Foreign Office, if our representatives have to be appointed by the Foreign Office, and if, as I know, the treaty has been submitted to the Imperial Government before being signed and put into force? Really there is something wrong as to this claim of our enjoying equality of status. We are a sister nation but the big sister has still more power than the younger one.

There is nothing
wrong in the making of the treaty; the only wrong is in the humbug of professing to us that there has been any change in the status of Canada. Canada is growing bigger and more important every day in the eyes of the Empire and in the eyes of the world as well-that much is true. Beyond that, all this talk about a change of status is absolute rubbish-that is the only thing that is wrong. My hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) states that His Maiesty has sanctioned these appointments. It is true that His Majesty's name is in the Bill, but in this treaty there is no reference to His Majesty from beginning to end. My right hon. friend said there was no formality in the making of treaties before but he is mistaken. He is mistaken in bis reference to the Washington agreement. That was not signed by the British Ambassador at Washington but by representatives of Canada on the one side and those of United States on the other, -but it was not in the form of a treaty. If it had been a treaty it would probably have received the signature of those designated by His Majesty strictly for that purpose.
But that also was done with the privity of the British Ambassador at Washington.

With the knowledge of the ambassador, who gave us every help he could. But when my hon. friend says there is no formality, I want to call attention to the fact that there is a great lack of formality, and that is one of the amazing things. Iii the document itself from A to Z there is not any reference to His Majesty, there is nothing to show whether it is made by His Majesty or not, unless this " H.M.S. Ambassador " on one of the printed documents and not on the other refers to His Majesty. The French Convention Act made in 1907 sets forth in the schedlue to the Act:
His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and of the British Dominions beyond the Seas, Emperor of India, and the President of the French Republic, being desirous of improving and extending the commercial relations between .Canada and France, have resolved to conclude a Convention with that object and have named as their respective Plenipotentiaries, that is to say:-
His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and of the British Dominions beyond the Seas, Emperor of India,
His Excellency the Right Honourable Sir Freneis Leveson Bertie, Knight Grand Cross of the Most Distinguished Order of St. Michael and St. George, Knight Grand Cross of the Royal Victorian Order, Knight Commander of the Most Honourable Order of the Bath, His Majesty's Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the Government of the French Republic,-
What an undemocratic lot they were!

I should like to associate myself with every effort made by this Government or any other government of Canada along the line of nationhood. I do not see why Mr. Hardinge of Penshurst came into this matter at all. I do not see why the right hon. gentleman (Sir George Foster) our Minister of Trade and Commerce could not have done the whole thing himself, and I would have preferred to see him do it. Then we would not have had all this discussion about the meaning of "H.M.S." after the name of Mr. Hardinge of Penshurst.
You mean Lord Hardinge.

Yes. I can understand, of course, that the trade agreement could have been made nominally between the King and the President of the French Republic. He would act then as King of Canada, and the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce would act as the minister of the King of Canada. It is quite true that the agreement itself does not mention the name of the King. But I want to express the view, which I believe is entertained by the vast majority of the members of this House sitting on your left, Mr. Chairman, that we accept with pleasure any change of status which brings us to a position of equality. What we do find fault with is the pretension of the Government in words that equality has been achieved when their acts belie their words. I would have had the Minister of Trade and Commerce in Paris do just as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's did at the time of the reciprocity agreement with the United States.
They were doing two different things.

One was a treaty and the other was entering into an agreement which was not a treaty but merely an agreement for concurrent legislation. I grant that. But after all, both the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce and the
hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's were dealing as representatives of Canada with a foreign power. In the case of Washington ten years ago the letter evidencing our part of the agreement directed to the Secretary of State of the United States was signed by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's himself without any intervention of the British Ambassador.
I can understand the feeling of impatience that the hon. member has when he hears loftly statements of equality of nationhood come from a Government which in its acts has not proceeded along the line of nationhood as far as he did himself by his act. It is true he does not like that direction, and of course his opinion is entitled to every respect which his patriotism and long experience merit. But I do want to say that the members on this side in large measure agree with the aspirations of the Government, and they only want them to be consistent and sincere and to carry themselves along this road not only by words but by deeds.
I wish only to say a word in view of one statement made by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's indicating that I would rather like to eliminate the name of His Majesty from our treaty.
His name is not in it.

It is not my sentiment, though. I want to keep the name of His Majesty in any treaty concerning Canada: but I want His Majesty to act through Canadian representatatives appointed by the Canadian Government without the intervention of the Foreign Office in London.

This is not a perfect treaty. All this may happen very shortly, because in the schedule I read this:
Pending the conclusion of a new commercial convention, with a view to which negotiations will begin immediately, the French and Canadian Governments have agreed to the following provisions.
So this is only temporary and before long we will have the old form.

I would like the minister to comply with the request of the hon. member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe to bring down the correspondence in this matter before it enters into another stage. He certainly will not think that is unreasonable.

I understand the schedule to consist of new articles that were not in the old treaty?

- 2140
Yes.
How was this list prepared? Did the minister take the advice of the Manufacturers' Association or of any [DOT] other Canadian parties engaged in trade or business? From whom did this list come?

It was certainly amusing and a little bit instructive to observe the passage of ideas among my hon. friends on the other side. If the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen s lives, as I hope he will, ten or twenty years _ longer he will be the finest example of the good old autocrat ever seen in this House. His influence will be good with hon. gentlemen on that side; it will curb the somewhat rapid ascent toward a complete democracy which would get rid of all autocratic or kingly affairs and ceremonies as quickly as possible and lead up to that halcyon time in the future which was viewed with the eye of faith if not of natural vision-the time when we should be utterly freed from all these trammels and when a real Canadian could go anywhere, arrange anything in the way of treaties, sign them as he pleased and make them effective no matter where King George was or any other king who sat upon the throne. Well, it does no harm for us to have these little ideas; considering the views advanced on both sides we shall make a pretty fair average when we come to our more mature life. But I hope we shall never come to the time when by any extension of ultra-democracy we shall find ourselves separated from the Empire of which we have long been so important a part. All this persiflage about changed status and that sort of thing is very nice to hear. The younger chaps like it, and we older men sometimes feel as if we had to say something to keep up our end of things. But under it all there is a strong spirit of utter and complete loyalty to British institutions and British constitutional forms. All this cavorting around and airing of our opinions helps to progress, but let us not cut the painter; let us ponder deeply whence we came and keep our eye, too, on the future, with regard to what is the best course for us there. When my hon. friend was reading out those sonorous titles there was, I am sure, a well defined reservation in his mind, sufficient to tame down such adventurous and reckless spirits as that of my hon. friend from Brome and keep them within the traces as [.Mr. Sinclair.]
we pass along the way to our national development.
Now, I was not in Paris trying to make a treaty; that it was impossible to do. I was simply trying to keep the way open to trade between France and Canada during these most strenuous and trying times. Perhaps I am not wrong in saying that France has had to bear greater burdens than any other nation, taking everything into account. She wants to retain for her own workmen as much work as possible she wants to prop herself up in every way that she can and lead up to that readjustment which lies before her, the attainment of which will strain her finances to the utmost. Nobody can go in there and sit down alongside those men and demand this or that; he feels more like giving them almost everything they ask. All I wanted to do, therefore, was to keep this business channel open as far as possible. Speaking frankly, I believe we have given in this little modus vivendi the advantage to France over ourselves. I do not quarrel with that; France gave us all that her statesmen could give us in this modus vivendi. When they took some things from us because they wanted to build up certain industries of their own, in these twelve articles particularly, I tried to get a counterbalance and they gave us this counterbalance which is shown in schedule 2. I had to judge from my own experience during twenty or thirty years of public life what things should be added to that list. Some of the articles are of considerable importance. So when this was put down as the very maximum of what could be granted, I assented to it and put my signature to the paper, and that was all there was to it. If it had been the formation of a permanent treaty which went into all matters in detail, that would have been a different thing. But this is something like a gentleman's agreement, with a view to our doing the best we can until the clouds clear and we can get together and come to a larger and more permanent arrangement. As to forms and things of that kind, is not the substance the main thing? What we did was to have Canadian sentiment and Canadian experience form the basis of the arrangement. The British Government made no cavil about it; after we had arranged it they instructed their ambassador to sign it and he did so as representing Great Britain. It is simply a modus vivendi, as I have said, an arrangement of a temporary character, and it was signed in the regular way. It did not have all the high-sounding names that might be assigned to a formal

treaty, but we have the substance, and that is the main thing.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3: Governor in Council may carry out provisions of agreement.

Does this clause not
vest a rather broad power in the Governor in Council? Of course, if it has been done in other cases I am not disposed to quarrel with it here.
It is the usual form.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On the schedule:
Schedule II should be amended by striking out the first "T" in the letters which follow items 522 and 525, leaving simply the letters "M.T."

I notice there is power vested in the Governor in Council in the usual form. I happen to have under my hand now the Act bringing into force the convention of 1908, and I find that it reads:
The Governor In Council may make such orders and regulations as are deemed necessary to carry out the provisions and intent of this Act and of the said convention.
The operation of all laws inconsistent with the giving to the provisions of the said convention and of this Act their full effect shall from time to time he suspended to the extent of such inconsistency.
But there is nothing in the Act confirming the other treaty to give the Governor in Council power to change it.
The Governor in Council may make such regulations as are deemed necessary to carry out the provisions and intent of this Act and of the said convention.
Why not stop there? Why give the Governor in Council power to make new laws from time to time?

The first subclause reads:
The Governor in Council may make such orders and regulations as are deemed necessary.
And so on.

To the first part I
take no objection.

Then it reads:
Any Order in Council or regulation made under this Act-
-that is, in accordance with the agreement -will have the same effect as if enacted
in the Act, that is, will have the same force in law.

What precedent has my right hon. friend for that? It is not in the preceding law, and it is giving the Governor in Council unusual powers. Before the Bill goes through my right hon. friend might look into that.

Yes. We do
not want any more powers than are necessary.
Before the third reading, my right hon. friend will bring down the correspondence?
I will see that fhat is brought down before we take the other stage.

Schedule agreed to.
Bill reported.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Civil Government-mines, salaries, and contingencies, $483,250.

Have we considered the
Estimates of the Department of Mines yet?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Department of
Mines forms part of the Department of the Interior. It is under the same minister. We have already gone into the Estimates of the Department of the Interior.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Before we
begin the discussion, I would like to ask my right hon. friend if he intends to keep the House very long this evening? We were here until half past two o'clock this morning.
Not very long, and we will take up Estimates to-morrow.

Normally, how many
men are employed in the Geological Survey, and how many men are now in the employ of that branch?

speechtext: There are 219 employees in the Mines Branch altogether and 55 vacancies at the present time. In the Geological Survey there are 115 employees at the present time, and when the department is working to its full limit we have 150.

How many of the
men in this department are being sent into what is known as the Fort Norman-Mackenzie district this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Four parties.
How are they being transported from Edmonton into that district?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
