Very largely by canoes,
by river and lake.
Why does the department continue a statistician on the pay roll when there is a chief statistician?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
He still remains in the
department, although his functions have been transferred to the Bureau of Statistics.

Is there not some attempt on the part of the Government to bring all the statistical branches within one department? They seem to have been at this now for two or three years. Will this office be transferred, or is it the intention to continue the branch in this department?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
This will be transferred
as soon as the Bureau of Statistics is prepared to take it.	.

That is not a very satisfactory answer, although it may be quite satisfactory from the minister's standpoint. The Bureau of Statistics was organized a few years ago. It seems to be very slow in getting in the different statisticians from other departments. What is the real trouble? Is it that the minister is not able to make this department a success and to get all these other statisticians under it?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The Bureau of Statistics now have some of their staff familiarizing themselves with what is going on in the Department of Mines, and just as soon as they are ready to take over that work, it will be taken over. We expect it will be completed in a short time.

Will it be completed
before next session?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am not a prophet, but I think there is every indication that it will be.
A man does not have to be a prophet to answer that if he is in control of a department. It is not necessarily a prophet's job at all.

The minister was
good enough to state the number of officials in the Geological Survey. Would he state into what divisions they are divided, and the number in each?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sure the committee would have no objection to the minister giving an answer. The chairman does not want to intervene except to say

that any lengthy discussion on this subject would not be strictly in order. There is a special item for the Geological Survey, which will be found on page 53 of the Estimates, and, of course, it is the duty of the Chairman to prevent the same discussion upon two seperate items.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There are ten divisions in the Geological Survey.	_
I should like to ask in connection with this item for inspector of explosives whether the department has investigated a new explosive known as Thompsonite?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have no information regarding any such explosive.

I should like to get an answer to my question. The minister has stated that there are ten divisions of the Geological Survey. As to the point the Chairman raised, I do not wish to enter into a discussion of matters that would come up under some other item, but the item we are now discussing is the salaries of the different members of the Mines division, which, of course, includes the geologists, and I therefore think my question would be in order.

I notice that we are asked to provide the salary for a junior purchasing agent. How many more purchasing agents are we going to have? Will this man still continue with the department or will he be merged with the new Purchasing Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There is only one purchasing agent in the department.

What is the nature of his work? Under closure we have voted one-sixth of the salaries for a Purchasing Commission, and I should like to know what necessity there is for retaining a purchasing agent in each department if we are going to have a commission to control the purchasing for all the departments.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
This purchasing agent
calls for tenders, assembles the work, and operates through the Purchasing Commission.

An I to understand that the purchasing agents in the different departments are to be continued, and that the Purchasing Commission is really a superfluous body created merely for the purpose of making jobs for certain friends of the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: This man is retained bemuse we find him useful.

I suggested to the Minister of Trade and Commerce a few minutes ago that as we sat until 2.30 this morning it would be advisable to adjourn after this item had passed. He is no longer in the House, but I should like to know whether the agreement stands with the other minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not hear the
agreement, but undoubtedly if the Minister of Trade and Commerce made it, we on this side will adhere to it.
He said: Yes, we will go into Supply to-morrow.

I think I am entitled to an answer to my question. I asked how many divisions there were in the Geological Survey, and how many officers there were in each division. I do not think that question refers to the item on page 53 at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not exactly rule the question out of order, but merely drew the attention of the committee to the fact that it would be well not to enter into any lengthy discussion on this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The divisions are as follows : drafting division, division of mineralogy, boring division, photographic division, geologists division, library division, topographical division, and the paleontological division.

Referring to the geologists division, what is the normal number of geologists employed by the department? I notice that we are providing salaries for eleven geologists. I understand that normally, when the department was running properly, there were more geologists than eleven.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There are 11 geologists' nositions, with 4 vacancies; 10 associate geologists, with 3 vacancies; 4 assistant geologists, with 2 vacancies.
Did these vacancies occur during last year, why did they occur, and why are they not being filled?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: They have occurred since April 1920. The positions have not been filled because up to the present time it has been found impossible to secure men possessing the necessary qualifications.

Due to the salary
offered?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is one of the reasons, I presume. .

Are there any other
reasons?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There has been a strong demand for geologists within the last year or so owing to various developments, particularly in oil, and the strongest demand has come from private corporations, which have been able to pay very much higher salaries than the Government has paid.

What is the regular
salary paid geologists by the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext:
And what is usually
paid by outside corporations?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
From $5,000 to $6,000,
and in some cases as high as $7,000.

Have any of these
men who have left the department gone into universities? If so, how many?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I understand that three have gone to universities.

There has been considerable discussion in this House on different occasions in regard to our natural resources. Now, before natural resources can be developed they must be discovered, and the work of the geological survey is to locate certain of our resources and give necessary information regarding them. This is a very important work and is being done in an excellent manner by the department, so far as they are able to accomplish any results with the staff they have. I understand that instead of 18 or 20 men, which is the number the staff should comprise, there are at present only 11, and this number is utterly inadequate to the necessity in a country like this. I am sure the department must be considerably handicapped at present. As the minister has shown, the salaries paid are altogether too low for the class of men required. I know instances of men in the Geological Survey, receiving salaries ranging from $2,300 to $2,700, who have left the department and gone into universities, getting, to start with, from $3,000 to $4,000, with the prospect of an increase to $6,000, and, in addition to this, five months off in the summer, during which they can earn from $1,500 to $3,000 by special work in their line. The universities are not noted for paying particularly high salaries, and surely an important department like this should be able to pay men of this class higher salaries than they can receive from

these institutions. I am informed that men have left the department to go into private concerns at much larger salaries than they were receiving from the department, although they would prefer working under the department if the remuneration they received were commensurate with the importance of the duties they perform, and bore some reasonable relation to the salaries they can get outside. There is a certain line of work in the department which attracts men of this stamp, and they are prepared to take a little less than is offered in mercantile pursuits; but the discrepancy is so great at present that these men have perforce to leave the department, and so their valuable services are lost to the country. The work of locating our natural resources is consequently retarded to a great extent; and, as I have said, unless we can locate those resources, we cannot develop them. I plead strongly for an increase in the salaries paid these highly technical experts, men who have spent years in the service, are graduates of universities, and have important degrees. It is in the interests of the department and of the Country generally that there should be a readjustment of the schedule of wages in this direction. I feel strongly about this matter, because I live in a part of the country where I come across the work which these geologists and their parties are carrying on, and I cannot too strongly emphasize the importance of their work.

Can the hon. gentleman
point to any resources or mines located by government engineers? That is .not their business; it is not their business to go prospecting.

4 I know an instance where a departmental geologist, in exploring certain territory where there were some mining properties, suggested that an investigation might profitably be made of a certain part of that territory. He was not a prophet and could not, of course, guarantee results, but on the strength of his suggestion, this investigation was made and very material and important results did follow. In other instances, territories are mapped out, the character of the land and the strata is set out in pamphlets, and this information is available to those interested. Frequently the dissemination of this information attracts people into some particular district, with the result that discoveries of no small importance are made.

I entirely disagree with the proposition of the hon. member that large salaries should be paid to university professors, whether they pose as geologists or not. It seems to me that the man in the district is the one who should receive consideration. Cobalt was discovered by a man who did not know the scientific nature of silver. He tripped on a bar of something in his rovings and took it to a commercial man who had the money to get it examined, and it was found to be silver. I would give the money to the man on the spot in the district, the man who prospects and who needs it.
The hon. member has not fairly stated my point, but that is immaterial. If he is right, why have technical experts at all? Why not rely on the men who discover these things by accident?

Technical experts have their place, but they have not the genius for exploration. They are paid good salaries under the segis of the Government, but the men in the far west and north, who have the spirit of adventure and discovery, are the men who have done the best work in the discovery of precious minerals. I would ask the Government, if they are going to do anything to help in the development of our resources, to look at the districts where minerals are found, see the intrepid men, the men with pluck, energy and courage, and give them some assistance or encouragement by way of bounty, so that they may go forth and add fresh laurels to their achievements. We have had a university man in the person of Professor McCallum, for some ten or twelve years, and I have been waiting all this time to discover what he has done.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Research work.

Yes, it is research, but we have never had any report, as to the results which have attended the payment of the moneys he has received from us.
I think my principle is right. If a university professor-already having a sinecure, identified with one of the great universities, having a salary sufficient to support himself and his family-is given a job beyond that which he already had, I think the very finest credentials should be put forward by him. I prefer to take the man who lives in the north and the west, who has done things himself, who has a passion for doing things, who has the spirit of adventure and discovery and I prefer to spend the country's money on that man rather

than to give it to any university professors because I have seen some of these university professors in the north. They go out with a pair of goggles, a leather mit, and a wonderful hammer made especially to crack rocks and they look wise; I have been struck with the appearance of wisdom that some of them possess. On the other hand I have seen the man that did the work and made, a record. That man whom perhaps somebody staked, has gone into the unknown and has got better results, with the expenditure of less money, than has the university professor.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I may [DOT] say in reply to the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell) that the department is already taking up the matter of salaries with the Civil Service Commission and we expect results very shortly.
Does the minister mean university professors?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not know whether they are university professors or not. We are not hiring university professors-field men are what this department is using.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I may say that I do not quite agree with the last speaker in not giving, perhaps as full credit to the scientific man in the field as is due him. Coming from the province of British Columbia I remember very well the very excellent and accurate work done by the late Dr. George M. Dawson, Chief Geologist of the Department of Mines. As a result of the work he did in British Columbia that province has been able to furnish prospectors with information which has materially assisted them to discover very fine locations of minerals that have proved paying properties. As I say the late Dr. Dawson did very excellent work, particularly in connection with our coal fields on Vancouver Island. Then again a geologist one of the Government men, in the case of the Ross-land mines, was able to give the owners certain information that has prolonged the life of those mines situated on the hill at Rossland, B.C. Furthermore, oil was located in the Mackenzie River basin by Mr. McConnell, another geologist, who was in the department over thirty years ago. I presume those oil discoveries would have been developed long before this, had it not been that the district was so difficult of access. A geologist for the department also located gypsum in northern Manitoba and the coal fields in Saskatchewan. Out in our
province we usually think that the work of assisting the prospector in the field comes within the purview of the Provincial Government rather than that of the Federal Department of Mines and they, look to the prospector, to some extent, in British Columbia to discover new districts containing minerals.

I would like to say to my hon. friend from North Perth that in my remarks I was not referring to university professors but to experts belonging to the Geological Survey Department. Following up the line taken by the minister I would say that I have in mind a certain ex-member of that department who spent several seasons in northern Manitoba, and who has given very valuable information to mining engineers and to prospectors generally-in fact the prospectors to whom such tribute was paid by my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy), were very loud in their praises of this particular gentleman because of the help he gave them in their work of looking for minerals in that country. As far as this ex-member of the Survey was concerned, I understand he had been working for the Government for approximately six years. He was a graduate of a Canadian University and received another degree from an overseas university. At the time he left the employ of the Government he was receiving the princely salary of $2,300 or thereabouts. He left to take a position in a university at a salary of $3,800 which will be increased annually to a considerable amount. The fact of the matter is these men cannot stay with the department under present conditions. The man to whom I refer was not in any way like the professors discribed by my hon. friend form North Perth; he was an actual worker in the field and did just as hard, onerous and arduous work as any of the prospectors in the country.

I do not wish to delay the passing of the item, but I would like to say that this is a subject that is discussed in the technical mining press, and every prospector and every mining engineer in the country is invited to condemn this Government because it does not increase the salaries of the members of the staff of the Geological Survey in order to keep them in the public service, rather than let them go to private companies. We ought to look at the matter from the point of view of the interests of the country at large-that is the right view for the committee to take. A man attached to the

Geological Survey here is not an expert in the same sense as a man who takes charge of practical mining operations. The man _in the department goes round to places where it is heard that discoveries have been made and takes maps of that section of the country. He goes over the various mines and describes them in reports, many of which you will find in the department here. That ends his work; he expresses no opinion to the public, and is not supposed to express any, as to whether these mines are of value or not. That is a very primitive way of dealing with the question. It is only within recent years that the department has gone to the length, following the lead of the United States and of the Ontario Government, of making what is known as topographical and geological surveys of these sections of the country where we have mines. That is now being done to some extent but it is not done generally; and knowing as I do, the volumes that are published by the department, I must say that for years thousands of dollars were spent by the geologists of the department in writing stories of the nice canoe trips they took on Great Slave lake, and other inland waters, where now everybody is finding oil. I am not casting any reflections on the department, no doubt it is serving its purpose, but the mine owners need men who will go down a mine and tell them where the fault is and where to find the ore. That is a different story altogether. These men that have left the department are taken away by mining corporations who want to have men in their service who will go down in their mines, who will examine their properties, and then give them practical advice. These men are following a much more useful occupation by being in private employ than being in the employ of this Government, although we would1 like particularly to have them.
I have failed yet to find out any substantial discovery made by the department. Their men may have told that they had seen signs of certain minerals or something of that kind. I know that geologists of the department have slammed .some of the best mining properties that we have in the country. Take the Helen mine in Michipi-coten. That was discovered by a Government geologist who reported the following winter that there were not more than eighteen inches of iron there and that the property would not amount to anything, although subsequently several millions of dollars worth of ore was taken out of the property. It is also well known that Gov-	.
ernment geologists predicted that Cobalt would only last about three years-that although there was conglomerate on the surface, silver did not exist in the lower strata. To-day millions of dollars are be- -ing taken out of that lower strata. It is the same all over. It is impossible for any man, unless he is employed in the actual operation of a mine, to go, as my hon. friend said "with a pair of goggles on and a hammer," and say, "this is going to be a mine or this is not going to be a mine." Nevertheless the action of the Government in having a staff of excellent men going over the country, making thorough geological and topographical maps and discovering the fractures of the earth, and all that sort of thing, is no doubt going to lead to great advances in the future. But there is nothing drawn so far as the department is concerned. I do not see how they could retain very high priced men to do this simple field work, which is of a purely superficial character, when there are lots of good companies that will pay those men high salaries to look after their mines.
What would be a fair salary for a field man?

I think the salary paid
by the department is fairly reasonable, $4,000.
They do not pay that; that is the point.
What do they pay them, $3,500?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext:
I knew that, because I . have been following the matter, as I say, in the Mining Journal. That is not a bad salary. There are many professional men, such as lawyers and doctors, who have spent just as much time in study and who in private practice are not able to make one-half that salary. For the work the Government demands the pay is excellent. But if the Government is to send experts to tell mine owners what to do with their mines, I do not think one half the owners would pay any attention to their advice. Those owners have their own views on mining matters. So far as discoveries are concerned, their mine superintendents understand their work thoroughly, and the history of mining shows that those are the men who make the actual discoveries. I do not say anything about the men who have left the department. They have been

added to the sum total of the operating forces of our mines, and the work they are doing now is much more useful to the country at large than if they were sitting in their departmental offices in Ottawa or going out surveying and smoking their pipes in their canoes.
But many of those men have gone out of the country.

My hon. friend has been speaking of the mines in his part of the country. There is one large mining property there, the Flin Flon, and it is said that when the ore in sight is worked out it is questionable whether the mine will pay for operation. The Mandy mine, which has produced millions of tons of ore containing a very high grade of copper, is said now to be practically exhausted, and I have no doubt that fifty per cent of the geologists who look at it will swear that not another pound of ore will be got from that mine.
Who says that?
I have seen that stated in the technical press.
Is the hon. gentleman aware of the price of copper to-day?

I know all about that just as well as the hon. gentleman does. I read the technial press. According to the information I gather from that press the so-called technical experts consider that the Mandy mine is played out.
It is not. '

The expert who went
over the Hollinger mine, which is to-day the greatest gold mine in the world, gave an adverse report to the McMartin Brothers, and it was only their courage and practical knowledge that decided them to develop the property, and they put $50,000,000 into it before they quit. With reference to coal mining, that is a little different, because it is largely surface work, and if a proper topographical survey is made something can be shown of what the result is likely to be. But there are coal mines in British Columbia where the experts said there were millions of tons of coal, but which after development, owing to crushers and squeezers, were found to be practically worthless. Nevertheless I say the technical experts of to-day are of great use to mine owners. Take the iron mines of Michigan and Wisconsin. The majority
of them were deserted a few years ago and it was said there was no more ore in them. Some of the mining professors of Wisconsin, who made a study of iron mining, came to the conclusion that the iron ore lay along certain contacts in those mines, and the diamond drill proved there were millions of tons of ore available; but there were other mines that the diamond drill went into without finding any ore. I do not think the department is to blame. We wish the men who have left every success, and when they get tired of working for private firms I hope the department will have good jobs ready for them. I am sorry I have occupied so much time, but I wanted to clarify the air.

I think the hon. gentleman who has just sat down should give his authority for the statement regarding certain mining properties in Manitoba, particularly the Flin Flon and the Mandy, because my information is entirely contrary to his. In my opinion his statements are entirely erroneous.
I hope they are.
They are.

I do not like the minister in charge of these Estimates, who is not the minister of the department, to get in wrong with the historical references in regard to oil. It is said to-night that a man named Caron-whom I do not know, but I presume he is a professor-has rendered great service to the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I referred to Mr. Mc-
Connell, the late deputy minister of the department.

Yes. It was said that
he had rendered great service to the department by locating oil in the Mackenzie Basin. I know that in the Interior Department and in the Statistical Branch there are unimpeachable records that Mackenzie, who gave his name to the Mackenzie river, nearly one hundred years ago found the natives gathering oil from the surface of pools, showing unmistakeable evidence that oil was superabundant there. That Mr. McConnell-I think he was a professor when he set up that claim-could thirty years ago put himself forward as discoverer of oil in that district would lead me to think that some one in the department had-to use a word that I do not intend to be offensive-been "stringing" the acting minister that he and not Mackenzie was the discoverer of these great oil districts. It seems to me there is just

that trouble in the departments here-I have seen it before in this House-that men to impress upon the ministers or acting ministers of their great value, set up claims that have no foundation in fact.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Ballantyne for the adjournment of the House:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understand the Government intend going on with Estimates to-morrow. Can the minister indicate what departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Whatever Government business is on the Order Paper will be advanced as well as the Estimates we have already entered upon, and in addition to those the Militia and Labour Estimates.

Might I suggest that
a general statement "whatever business is on the Order Paper will be advanced," is not very helpful. It would be desirable, if possible, on these occasions that some intimation should be given as to the particular business to be taken up. Some hon. members are specially interested in certain matters and not in others.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In regard to the Militia Estimates, do I understand that the minister intends that that should be
taken up by consent, or is it proposed to go into them without any consent?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I
really do not think this is the proper time, on the motion for the adjournment of
the House, which is not debatable, to discuss a point of order concerning the right that the Government may have to bring up certain Estimates at another sitting with or without consent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have no desire to press the question at the moment, but I think the Government should be willing to make matters as definite as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I thought I made it clear enough. I said we intended to take up some of the Estimates that we have already entered upon; then, if there is any reasonable time left, we would take up Militia and Labour Estimates.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 11.37 p.m.
Friday, April 15, 1921.
